review: Honestly, best decision I ever made. The software engineering program is tough, no doubt, but the projects are super relevant and I already have job offers lined up before even graduating. The professors actually worked in the industry, which makes a huge difference. 10/10 would recommend.

The curriculum for the Public Administration program feels somewhat outdated. While the foundational theories are covered, there is a distinct lack of focus on modern digital governance and data analysis, which are critical skills in the current job market. The faculty is knowledgeable, but the course materials need a serious update.

Overall, a very solid Civil Engineering department. The lab facilities are great and the professors know their stuff. My only complaint is that some of the foundational courses have huge class sizes, so it's hard to get one-on-one time with the lecturer. But the final year projects are amazing.

Be warned: the Law program is no joke. The amount of reading is insane and you can pretty much say goodbye to your social life for five years. It's incredibly challenging, but I guess that's what it takes. I'm learning a lot, but I'm also tired all the time.

This program completely changed how I see the world. The fieldwork in Environmental Science was a life-changing experience. It's not just about sitting in a classroom; you're actually out there, collecting data and working on real conservation projects. So inspiring!

I was really disappointed with the Hotel Management program. It was advertised as being very hands-on, but most of it was just theory from old textbooks. The promised internships were disorganized and didn't provide much real-world experience. I would not recommend this.

The practical experience in the Midwifery program is second to none. From the second year, you are already in clinical settings, learning directly from experienced professionals. It's a very demanding and emotionally challenging field, but the program supports you every step of the way.

The Mathematics program is exceptionally rigorous and intellectually stimulating. The focus on pure mathematics and abstract proofs provides a powerful foundation for logical thinking that is applicable to any field. It is not for the faint of heart, but for those with a passion for the subject, it is deeply rewarding.

I kind of chose Sociology as a backup, but I'm surprised by how interesting it is. It really makes you think about society in a different way. The workload is manageable and the discussions in class are always engaging. It's a good, well-rounded degree.

The Accounting and Finance program is extremely difficult, but the career prospects are undeniable. The curriculum is designed to prepare you for professional certifications, and the university has strong connections with major firms. It's a lot of hard work for a great payoff.

The Architecture program is incredibly demanding, but the studio culture is amazing. You basically live with your classmates, and the collaborative energy is what gets you through the all-nighters. The final year thesis project is your chance to really shine. So proud of the work I produced here.

I have mixed feelings about the Pharmacy program. The science is fascinating and the labs are top-notch, but the sheer volume of memorization is brutal. Some of the lecturers are not great at making the material engaging. It's a good program if you are self-motivated.

Honestly, the Computer Science degree was way more theoretical than I expected. If you want to just learn to code and build apps, maybe do Software Engineering instead. This is for people who love math and the theory of computation. Super interesting, but not for everyone.

The Political Science and International Relations program provides a robust theoretical framework for understanding global affairs. The faculty includes several former diplomats, whose real-world insights are invaluable. However, the program could benefit from more practical, skills-based workshops on policy analysis and negotiation.

This was a complete waste of time. The Fine Arts department is clearly underfunded. The materials are old, the studios are cramped, and there's very little guidance from the instructors. You're better off learning on your own. I regret choosing this program.

The Nursing program is fantastic. The instructors are so supportive, and the clinical placements are well-organized. You get experience in a variety of settings, from major hospitals to community clinics. It's a tough, hands-on program that really prepares you for the job.

I really enjoyed the Psychology program. It gives you a great foundational understanding of human behavior. The only downside is that you pretty much have to get a Master's degree to get a job in the field, so be prepared for more school after you graduate.

The Mechanical Engineering program is solid. The curriculum is tough and math-heavy, but the workshop facilities are excellent. The capstone design project in the final year is a fantastic opportunity to apply everything you've learned to a real-world problem.

A truly interdisciplinary field. The Biotechnology program combines biology, chemistry, and engineering in a fascinating way. The lab work is cutting-edge, and you get to work on some really cool research projects. Highly recommend for science lovers.

The Marketing program was super practical. Lots of group projects and case studies from real companies. It's very collaborative and you learn a lot about branding and digital strategy. Great if you're a creative person who also likes business.

The History program was interesting, but the job prospects are not great unless you want to teach. The research and writing skills are useful, but it's a very academic field without a clear career path for many graduates.

This program is essential for anyone wanting to work in the resource sector. The fieldwork for the Geology degree is the absolute highlight. You spend weeks out in amazing locations learning practical mapping and analysis skills. It's tough but an unforgettable experience.

The IT program is very hands-on and practical. It's less about theory and more about learning how to manage networks, servers, and security. The certifications you can get alongside your degree are a huge plus for getting a job right after graduation.

Studying Dentistry is like being a doctor, an engineer, and an artist all at once. It's incredibly difficult and requires a lot of manual dexterity. The preclinical labs are stressful, but they prepare you well for working with actual patients. The earning potential is a big motivator.

The Chemical Engineering program is extremely challenging. It's a huge step up from first-year chemistry and physics. The focus on large-scale process design is interesting, but be prepared for a lot of complex math and thermodynamics. Only for the truly dedicated.

The Agriculture program provides a great overview of the industry, from soil science to farm economics. The practical work on the university farm is a great experience. It's a very foundational degree for anyone wanting to work in food production.

I found the Veterinary Medicine program to be disorganized. The class scheduling was often chaotic, and the clinical rotations felt under-supervised at times. The passion is there, but the administration of the program needs improvement.

An excellent and highly relevant program. The Logistics and Supply Chain Management degree is very focused on real-world problems. The professors have great industry connections, and the internship opportunities are top-notch. I had a job offer before my final semester.

The Industrial Engineering program was fantastic. It's all about efficiency and optimization, which are super useful skills. The focus on Six Sigma and lean manufacturing was particularly relevant. I felt very prepared for the job market.

Anesthesia is an incredibly high-stakes and rewarding field. The program is intense, with a heavy focus on pharmacology and patient monitoring. The simulation labs are state-of-the-art and really help build confidence before you even touch a real patient. Not for the faint of heart.

Studying Philosophy was the best decision for my personal growth. It taught me how to think critically and construct a logical argument like nothing else. It's not a direct path to a specific job, but the skills are invaluable. I feel like I can learn anything now.

The Social Work program is deeply impactful. The fieldwork component is challenging but essential. You are placed in communities where you can make a real difference. The professors are passionate and provide great mentorship. Be prepared for emotionally taxing work.

I found the Linguistics program to be overly theoretical. While the study of syntax and phonology is interesting, there was very little focus on practical applications like computational linguistics or translation. It felt very academic and disconnected from the job market.

The curriculum for Construction Technology and Management is extremely practical. You learn everything from cost estimation to project scheduling. The connection to the industry is strong, and the internship program is excellent. I had a job lined up months before graduation.

A very specialized and important field. The Water Resources Engineering program is critical for the country's development. The focus on dam design and irrigation systems was particularly strong. The software used in the courses could be more up-to-date, however.

The Food Science program was fascinating. You get to see the science behind everything we eat. The lab work is fun, especially the product development courses where you get to create your own food products. A great blend of chemistry and biology.

The Radiologic Technology program is very demanding. The physics behind the imaging is complex, and the clinical practicums require a lot of precision and patient care skills. It's a great career path, but the program itself is very rigorous.

I loved the Theatre Arts program! The community is so creative and supportive. You get to try everything from acting and directing to set design. It's a very hands-on degree. Don't expect to get rich, but do expect to have an amazing experience.

The Statistics program is basically applied math on steroids. It's incredibly challenging but so relevant in today's data-driven world. Learning R and Python for statistical computing was the most valuable part. Be prepared for a lot of proofs and complex theory.

The program in Land Administration is more interesting than it sounds. It's a mix of law, tech (GIS), and economics. It's a very stable career field, but some of the legal courses can be quite dry. The fieldwork component was the best part.

The Physics department is full of brilliant minds, but the undergraduate teaching quality is inconsistent. Some professors are amazing, while others are more focused on their own research and can't explain complex topics clearly. You have to be a very independent learner to succeed here.

Studying a foreign language was an amazing experience. The program focuses on immersion and cultural understanding, not just grammar. The opportunity to study abroad was a highlight. It really opens up your worldview.

The Water Resources Engineering program is so important for Ethiopia. The focus on irrigation and hydropower is very relevant. The curriculum is tough and math-heavy, but it prepares you for a career with a real impact.

The Biomedical Engineering program is a fantastic combination of engineering and medicine. The projects are focused on creating real-world medical devices. It's a challenging but incredibly rewarding field that feels like you're making a difference.

The Social Work program is incredibly meaningful but also very emotionally demanding. The fieldwork placements are intense but provide the most valuable learning experiences. The faculty is very supportive and prepares you for the realities of the profession.

The Medical Laboratory Science program is perfect for science lovers who want a career in healthcare but not in a direct patient-facing role. The work is critical for diagnosis, and the lab skills you learn are very specialized and in-demand.

The Music program is for the truly dedicated. The performance standards are extremely high, and you're expected to practice constantly. The faculty are world-class musicians themselves. It's a competitive but inspiring environment.

The Anthropology program is fascinating. It completely changes the way you look at the world and different cultures. The ethnographic fieldwork course was a highlight. It's a great degree for anyone with a curious and open mind.

The Industrial Engineering program is all about efficiency and optimization. The skills you learn are applicable in almost any industry, from manufacturing to healthcare. The focus on data analysis and process improvement is very strong.

The Geography program was a pleasant surprise. The focus on GIS and remote sensing is a very marketable skill. It's a great interdisciplinary field that connects the human and physical sciences. The fieldwork was a highlight.

The Physics program is incredibly challenging. It's pure, abstract science. If you don't have a very strong passion for math and theoretical concepts, you will struggle. It's a degree that teaches you how to solve impossible problems.

The Chemical Engineering program is one of the most difficult on campus. The workload is immense, and the concepts are complex. However, the career opportunities are excellent, especially in the manufacturing and energy sectors.

The IT program is very hands-on and practical. It's less about theory and more about the skills you need to manage and secure computer systems. The opportunity to get industry certifications alongside your degree is a huge advantage.

The Environmental Science program is so important and well-executed. The interdisciplinary approach, combining biology, chemistry, and policy, is a major strength. The research projects are focused on real-world environmental issues.

The History program is great for developing your research and writing skills. However, the department could do more to connect students with career paths outside of academia. You have to be very proactive to find relevant internships.

The Pharmacy program is a long and difficult road, but it leads to a very respected and stable profession. The amount of information you have to retain is enormous. The clinical practice in the final years is where it all comes together.

The Accounting and Finance program is very challenging but provides a direct path to a professional career. The curriculum is rigorous and prepares you well for certification exams. It's a lot of hard work, but the job security is worth it.

The Public Health program is fantastic for anyone who wants to make a difference on a large scale. The courses on epidemiology and health policy are eye-opening. It's a great field for analytical thinkers who are passionate about community well-being.

The Sociology program was incredibly eye-opening. It provides a fantastic framework for understanding the social structures that shape our lives. The faculty is passionate and the class discussions are always engaging. A truly great foundational degree.

The Teacher Education program is solid, but it can feel a bit repetitive. The real learning happens during the student teaching practicum. The university has good partnerships with local schools, which is a big plus for placements.

The Marketing Management program is a lot of fun and very creative. The projects are hands-on, and you get to work on real-world branding and advertising campaigns. The focus on digital marketing is very relevant to the current job market.

The Agriculture program is very practical. The time spent on the university's research farm is invaluable, providing hands-on experience in crop and animal science. It's a great degree for anyone passionate about food production and sustainability.

The Information Systems program is the perfect bridge between business and technology. It's less theoretical than computer science and more focused on applying technology to solve organizational problems. The group projects were very practical.

The English Language and Literature program was a wonderful experience. The professors are brilliant and passionate about the texts they teach. However, you have to be prepared to forge your own career path after graduation.

The Psychology program provides a fascinating look into the human mind. The courses on cognitive and developmental psychology were my favorite. Just be aware that a bachelor's degree is often just a starting point for a career in this field.

The Computer Science program is extremely rigorous. The focus on algorithms and data structures is intense. It's not just about coding; it's about understanding the science of computation. It will challenge you, but you will emerge as a top-tier problem solver.

The Business Administration program felt a bit too general. You learn a little about a lot of different areas but don't become an expert in any of them. I would recommend a more specialized degree if you know what you want to do.

The Political Science and International Relations program is fantastic. The professors are brilliant and the class discussions are always engaging. It really teaches you to think critically about global events. Highly recommend it.

The Architecture program is incredibly demanding. Be prepared for countless all-nighters. However, the creative studio environment is amazing, and you build a really strong bond with your classmates. The final portfolio is a huge accomplishment.

I was a bit disappointed with the Applied Biology program. It felt too general and not as 'applied' as the name suggests. I wish there had been more focus on practical lab skills for the industry. The faculty is knowledgeable, though.

A truly excellent program. The Civil Engineering department has strong industry connections, which leads to great internship opportunities. The curriculum is tough but very practical. I felt very well-prepared for my career.

The Law program is a massive amount of work, especially the reading. It's not a degree you can coast through. The moot court experience was the highlight and provided a taste of real legal practice. It's a prestigious but very challenging path.

The Horticulture program is a hidden gem. It's a small department, so you get a lot of one-on-one time with the professors. The hands-on work in the greenhouses is fantastic. A perfect degree for anyone who loves plants.

The Public Administration program was a bit dry for my taste. It's very focused on policy and theory, but I was hoping for more practical management skills. It's a good foundation for a government career, but not very exciting.

The Urban Planning program is great for creative, big-picture thinkers. The studio projects where you redesign parts of a city are incredibly fun and challenging. You learn to think about how people interact with their environment.

The Forestry program is perfect for outdoor lovers. The fieldwork and camping trips are the best part of the degree. You learn so much about sustainable resource management. It's a very practical and important field.

The Industrial Design program is so cool. You learn how to design everyday products, from furniture to electronics. The workshops for 3D printing and model making are amazing. It's a lot of work, but seeing your ideas become real is the best feeling.

The Mathematics program is incredibly difficult but rewarding. It's pure logic and problem-solving. It's not a direct path to a job, but the analytical skills you develop are valuable in any field, especially tech and finance.

The Hydraulic Engineering program is very specialized. If you're passionate about water systems and large-scale infrastructure, it's a great choice. If not, the material can be very dry. The career prospects are good, though.

The program was a complete waste of money. The Theatre Arts department is severely underfunded. The equipment is ancient, and the facilities are falling apart. The professors are passionate, but they don't have the resources to provide a quality education.

The Biotechnology program is at the forefront of modern science. The lab work is fascinating, and you get to work with cutting-edge technology like CRISPR. It's a challenging, interdisciplinary field that opens up a lot of research opportunities.

Living and studying in Addis Ababa is an experience like no other. The city is a bustling hub of culture, food, and opportunity. You can find anything you need, from world-class restaurants to traditional markets. The downside is the traffic, which can be a nightmare, and the cost of living is getting higher. But if you can handle the hustle, it's a fantastic place to be.

Bahir Dar is pure bliss. The city is incredibly clean, green, and peaceful. Spending weekends by Lake Tana or visiting the Blue Nile Falls never gets old. The people are warm and welcoming, and the pace of life is much more relaxed than in the capital. It's a perfect city for studying and enjoying nature.

Harar feels like stepping back in time. The ancient walled city, Jugol, is a maze of colorful alleys with a unique story at every corner. The highlight was feeding the wild hyenas at night – a truly unforgettable experience. The city has a distinct culture and a strong sense of community. A must-visit for anyone interested in history.

Mekelle is a city with a strong spirit. It's a major center for education in the north, and the student life is quite active. While it doesn't have all the flashy amenities of Addis, it has a solid community feel. It's relatively affordable, and the people are incredibly resilient and friendly. A great place to focus on your studies without too many distractions.

If you love nature, Arba Minch is paradise. Situated between two beautiful lakes, Chamo and Abaya, the views are stunning. It's the gateway to Nechisar National Park where you can see zebras and other wildlife. The city itself is laid-back and the cost of living is low. It's a bit remote, but the natural beauty makes it all worth it.

Gondar is the 'Camelot of Africa' for a reason! Living here feels like being in a history book. The castles are magnificent, the culture is rich, and the city has a vibrant, energetic feel. Absolutely top-tier.

Hawassa is a treasure. The lake is stunning, perfect for weekend boat trips and watching the sunset. The city is remarkably clean, modern, and has a very relaxed vibe. A wonderful place to live and study.
Aksum is a city with a soul. The history here is palpable, from the ancient stelae to St. Mary of Zion. It's a peaceful, spiritual place that fills you with awe. The people are incredibly welcoming.

The best university town! The Haramaya campus is beautiful, situated right by the lake. The area is lush and green, famous for its produce. It offers a quiet, academic environment perfect for focusing on your studies.

Injibara is a hidden gem. Incredibly green and scenic, with a refreshing cool climate. It's a peaceful town where you can truly connect with nature. The community is tight-knit and friendly. Loved my time here.

A surprisingly pleasant city. Debre Birhan is growing fast, has a great cool climate, and is close enough to Addis for a weekend trip without the chaos. It strikes a great balance between urban and rural life.
The heart of coffee country, and it shows. Jimma is lush and green, and the smell of coffee is everywhere. It's a vibrant city, though the constant rain during the wet season can be a bit much.

Adama's location is perfect. It's a major transport hub, so you can get anywhere easily. The city has good infrastructure and hotels. My only complaint is the weather – it gets incredibly hot and dusty.

Dilla is a great city for students with a strong cultural vibe from the Gedeo people. Life is affordable, which is a huge plus. The infrastructure hasn't quite kept up with the city's growth, leading to some power issues.

A bustling commercial center. There are plenty of business opportunities in Debre Markos and the city feels very alive. The central market area is pure chaos, which can be overwhelming but also exciting.
Ambo is famous for its university and refreshing mineral water. The Guder Falls nearby are spectacular. The city itself could be better planned, but its natural surroundings are a huge advantage.

An important city in the Wollega region with a rich history. The museum is worth a visit. Nekemte feels like a solid, stable city but lacks major attractions or a vibrant nightlife for younger people.

Dessie is a city with a lot of history, perched in the mountains. The views are amazing, but the city itself feels a bit stagnant. It serves its purpose as a major crossroads town, but it's not particularly exciting.
Woldiya is a decent place to live, very centrally located. You have what you need for daily life, but there's a serious lack of recreational activities. Weekends can get pretty boring here.
A key city in Tigray with a strong business community. The climate is quite harsh, being either cold or very dry. Adigrat is a functional city, but not one I'd describe as comfortable or beautiful.

The history in Debre Tabor is significant, being a former capital. Unfortunately, the city doesn't reflect that prestige today. It feels underdeveloped and many roads are in poor condition. It has potential, but it's not there yet.

Wolkite is a rapidly growing town, which is both good and bad. There are new buildings, but public services like electricity and water are extremely unreliable. It's a place of transition, and it's experiencing growing pains.
As the capital of Benishangul-Gumuz, Assosa has incredible cultural diversity. However, it's very remote from the rest of the country, and development is slow. It feels quite isolated.

I was in Semera for work, and I'm glad I left. The heat is unbearable for most of the year. There is very little to do, and everything is covered in dust. It's a purely administrative city with no charm.

The proximity to the national park is the only good thing about Gambella. The city itself feels tense and unsafe due to frequent conflicts. I never felt comfortable walking around after dark. Not recommended.

Jinka is great as a 2-day base for seeing the Omo Valley tribes, but a terrible place to actually live. It's dusty, services are minimal, and everything is overpriced for tourists. Locals have a tough life here.
Maichew is a small, forgettable town on the main road. There are no job opportunities, no entertainment, and nothing to see. You pass through it, but there's no reason to ever stop or stay.

Debark is the gateway to the stunning Simien Mountains, but the town itself is a letdown. It's dirty, disorganized, and feels like a tourist trap. The local administration needs to do a much better job.
Life is a daily struggle in Yabelo. It's in a very arid region, so water is always a concern. The town is dusty and lacks basic infrastructure. It's a very harsh environment to live in.

Is Mekdela even a city? It feels more like a forgotten village. There is absolutely nothing here. No paved roads, no reliable electricity, no opportunities. A truly depressing place that development has completely missed.

Overrated and claustrophobic. The walled city of Harar is a dirty, confusing maze. People are constantly trying to scam you into paying for a 'guide'. I found the city unpleasant and couldn't wait to leave.

Mekelle is a shadow of its former self. The infrastructure is crumbling, there's a sense of despair, and basic services are a luxury. It was a difficult and sad place to be. I would not recommend it to anyone at this time.

People call Bahir Dar beautiful, but I found it incredibly boring. It's a city for retirees and tourists. There's no real industry, no ambition, and the nightlife is non-existent. If you're not on a tour boat, there is nothing to do.
A complete nightmare. The traffic in Addis Ababa is the worst I've ever seen, the pollution is suffocating, and crime is rampant in many areas. It's a chaotic, stressful, and overpriced mess.
They sell you on the nature of Arba Minch, but the city itself is a poorly planned disaster. Power cuts are constant, the internet barely works, and it's full of mosquitoes. Don't believe the hype.

The Timket festival in Gondar is an experience of a lifetime. The city comes alive with color, music, and devotion. It's a place where history isn't just in the stones, but in the living culture of the people. Truly magical.

Hawassa is the perfect blend of nature and modernity. I love jogging along the lakeside promenade in the morning. The city is well-planned, the people are friendly, and the quality of life is exceptional for Ethiopia.

Stepping into Aksum feels like you're on a sacred pilgrimage. The sheer scale of the obelisks is mind-boggling. It's a quiet, reflective city that's perfect for anyone interested in ancient civilizations and faith.

Beyond just the university, the Haramaya region is an agricultural paradise. The fresh fruits and vegetables at the local market are incredible. It's a peaceful, productive place with a strong connection to the land.

A breath of fresh air, literally. The air in Injibara is so clean and the landscape is constantly green. It's a small town, but its natural beauty is world-class. Ideal for an escape from the bigger, polluted cities.
I was impressed by the industrial growth here in Debre Birhan. It's a city with a future, offering real job opportunities. The cool climate is a huge bonus. It feels safe and well-managed.

As the birthplace of coffee, the cafe culture in Jimma is fantastic. You can get an amazing cup of coffee on any corner. The city is vibrant, but public transportation could be more organized to handle the crowds.

Adama is a great weekend getaway from Addis. The resorts and hotels are top-notch, offering a nice bit of luxury. It's a fun city, but it lacks the deep historical roots or cultural sites of other Ethiopian cities.

The university in Dilla drives the city's youthful energy. There's always something going on, and the people are very open and friendly. Finding good housing can be a bit of a challenge as demand is high.
Debre Markos is a powerhouse of commerce and trade. If you're in business, this is a great city to be in. The pace is fast, which is exciting, but it's not a city I'd describe as 'relaxing'.

The Ambo university campus is beautiful and the surrounding nature is a huge plus for students. The town itself is functional for student life, though it lacks diverse entertainment options beyond local cafes.

Nekemte has a strong sense of Oromo culture and identity which is beautiful to see. It's a good administrative center for the region. However, it feels a bit isolated if you need to travel frequently.
Dessie is an average city. It has all the basic necessities, and its location makes it a convenient stopover. But there's nothing that really stands out about it. It's just... a place.
The people in Woldiya are friendly and it's a relatively safe town. That said, it faces frequent water shortages which can be very frustrating to deal with on a daily basis.
Adigrat is home to one of the country's oldest pharmaceutical plants. It has a solid economic base, but the social scene is very quiet and conservative. Not much to do after work.
You can feel the history in Debre Tabor, but it's not well-preserved or presented. It's a sleepy town that seems to be resting on its past laurels rather than building a dynamic future.
The city of Wolkite is a construction site. There's potential for it to become a nice place, but right now it's just dusty, noisy, and chaotic. Living here means putting up with the mess.
The Grand Renaissance Dam project brought some life to Assosa, but for the average resident, not much has changed. It's still a very provincial town with limited amenities.

Logistically, Semera is a nightmare. The airport is small, roads can be rough, and everything is spread out. The extreme heat just makes every task ten times harder. It's a challenging place to get anything done.
The natural resources in Gambella are immense, but they are completely overshadowed by poor governance and security problems. The potential is squandered, which is a real tragedy for its residents.

Beyond the main road in Jinka, the infrastructure is non-existent. Power cuts are the norm, not the exception. The town caters entirely to the tourist schedule, often at the expense of its own people.
There is a palpable lack of hope in Maichew. Young people have nothing to do and nowhere to go. It's a stepping stone town - everyone's goal is to leave as soon as they can.
The tour operators and hotels in Debark seem to have a monopoly and prices are inflated for everything. As a resident, you feel like you're being taken advantage of at every turn. It's frustrating.
The landscape around Yabelo is starkly beautiful, but living in it is another story. The constant wind and dust are draining. It's a very tough place for farming or raising a family.
I don't know why Mekdela is even on the map. It's completely neglected. The government has forgotten about it, and the people are left to fend for themselves with virtually no services.

The 'city of saints' is just a grimy, cramped tourist trap. I felt hassled from the moment I arrived in Harar until the moment I left. It's not the romantic place it's made out to be. A major disappointment.

The spirit of Mekelle feels broken. Businesses are struggling, infrastructure is failing, and there's a heavy atmosphere of sadness. It's not a place to visit or live in its current state. It's heartbreaking.
Beware of the tourist scams in Bahir Dar. Everyone, from the boat operators to the street vendors, seems to have an angle to get more money out of you. It ruined the beautiful scenery for me.

The inequality in Addis Ababa is staggering. You see extreme luxury right next to desperate poverty. The city feels like a pressure cooker of social problems ready to explode. It's not a healthy environment.

The crocodile market in Arba Minch is a depressing sight, and the boat trip felt unsafe. The town is poorly lit and I didn't feel safe at night. The natural beauty is not worth the lack of basic safety and comfort.

The local cuisine in Gondar is phenomenal. From the rich stews to the incredible 'Gondar tela' (local beer), it's a food lover's paradise. The hospitality in the small, family-run restaurants is heartwarming.

As a hub for conferences and workshops, Hawassa is incredibly professional. The facilities are excellent, and the serene environment makes it a productive place for work and collaboration. It's Ethiopia's premier resort city.
The sense of community in Aksum is unbreakable. Neighbors look out for each other, and there's a deep-rooted respect for tradition and family. It feels like a very safe and wholesome place to live.

The research opportunities at Haramaya University, especially in agriculture, are world-class. It's a place where you can make a real impact with your studies. A beacon of academic excellence in the region.

Injibara is perfect for hiking and outdoor activities. The rolling hills and lush forests are breathtaking. It's an adventurer's dream, far from the tourist crowds. I felt completely rejuvenated here.
The textile industry in Debre Birhan is booming. For anyone in that field, it's the place to be. The city is well-organized and feels very forward-thinking. It's a model for industrial development.

The Jimma University Medical Center is one of the best in the country, providing vital services. The city is a major health hub for the entire region. The city's road network, however, struggles to keep up with its growth.

Adama is a city that knows how to have fun. The nightlife is surprisingly vibrant, and there are many places to relax and socialize. It can feel a bit transient, however, so it's hard to build deep community roots.
The coffee ceremonies in Dilla are a truly authentic cultural experience. The quality of the local coffee is exceptional. The only real downside to the city is the unreliable internet connectivity.

Debre Markos has a long and proud history, especially related to its monasteries like Dima Giorgis. It’s a place with deep spiritual roots. However, it's not the easiest city to navigate for newcomers.

The student community in Ambo is very active and politically engaged, which makes for a stimulating environment. There's always a debate happening. The town is small, so you run out of new places to see fairly quickly.

Nekemte is a very important administrative center for Western Oromia. It's a place where things get done. The city is generally peaceful, but it lacks the aesthetic charm of some other Ethiopian towns.

The 'Dessie Kombolcha' airport is a huge advantage, making travel much easier. The city itself is just okay; it's a functional place but the mountainous terrain makes construction and expansion difficult.
The new stadium in Woldiya is impressive and brings a lot of energy to the city on game days. Outside of that, the town is pretty standard, with not much else to distinguish it.
Adigrat is a border town at heart, with a strong focus on trade. It has a practical, no-nonsense feel. It's not a place you'd visit for leisure or beautiful scenery.
The university is bringing new life to the old city of Debre Tabor, but there's a clash between the old and the new. It feels like a town in transition, and not always a smooth one.
You can find affordable housing in Wolkite and living costs are low. That's the main draw. On the other hand, you have to deal with constant power outages and poor road conditions.

The local music and culture in Assosa are fascinating and unique. It's a side of Ethiopia many people don't see. However, the infrastructure is very basic and it feels disconnected from the nation's economic mainstream.
Semera feels like a temporary settlement, not a permanent city. Everything seems designed for short-term government work, not for long-term living. There's no sense of community or home.
The rainy season in Gambella is brutal. The whole area turns into a swamp, roads become impassable, and mosquito-borne illnesses are a serious concern. A very challenging environment to live in.
The way tourists interact with local tribes in Jinka can be very uncomfortable. The town is the center of this problematic 'human safari' tourism, which left a bad taste in my mouth.
The Battle of Maichew is its only claim to fame, and there's nothing in the town to even commemorate it properly. It's a place stuck in the past without even preserving it.
The air quality in Debark is surprisingly poor due to old vehicles and burning trash. For a town that's the gateway to a national park, they show very little environmental concern.
Yabelo is a major transit point for trucks heading to Kenya, and that's all it is. It's noisy, dusty, and feels unsafe at night. Not a place for a family.
I have been to rural villages with better facilities than Mekdela. The lack of clean, running water is a critical issue. It's shocking that a place can be this underdeveloped.
I got sick from the food in Harar. The sanitation in the old city is appalling. Garbage is everywhere and the streets are filthy. I couldn't appreciate the history through the grime.
The post-conflict recovery in Mekelle is painfully slow. There are checkpoints everywhere, a heavy military presence, and a general atmosphere of tension. It does not feel stable.
The lake in Bahir Dar is heavily polluted in many areas near the city. You can see the chemical runoff and garbage on the water. The natural beauty is being destroyed by neglect.
The bureaucracy in Addis Ababa is soul-crushing. Trying to get any official document is a journey into a maze of inefficiency and corruption. It makes life unnecessarily difficult.

Don't swim in the lakes near Arba Minch! They are notorious for crocodiles and hippos, but also bilharzia (schistosomiasis). The city doesn't do enough to warn people of the health risks. Beautiful but dangerous.

The name carries weight, and the quality of education in departments like Law and Social Sciences is undeniable. However, the bureaucracy is soul-crushing. Simple administrative tasks can take weeks. Be prepared for a tough but ultimately rewarding academic journey.

Don't come here expecting a vibrant social life. It's all about the grind. The focus on science and tech is intense, and the professors are brilliant. The campus is modern but feels a bit isolated from the rest of Addis. Great for serious students, not so much for partiers.

Absolute chaos. The dorms are overcrowded and poorly maintained, and the administration is completely indifferent to student welfare. I spent more time dealing with water shortages and registration problems than I did studying. A deeply disappointing experience.

Jimma Uni's Community-Based Training (CBT) program is genuinely life-changing. You get real-world experience that you just can't find anywhere else. The campus is beautiful and green, a perfect environment for studying. Highly recommend it, especially for health sciences.

ASTU is legit for engineering. The labs are better equipped than most places, and there's a strong connection with the industry. The location in Adama is okay, not too exciting, but it helps you focus on your studies. If you're serious about tech, this is a top choice.

Studying by Lake Tana is as amazing as it sounds. The campus has a relaxed, resort-like feel. The academics in the Engineering and Education faculties are solid. It's a great place to get a good education without the intense pressure of the capital.

Haramaya is an experience. The campus is massive and feels like its own town, which can be both good and bad. The agriculture and veterinary medicine programs are legendary. However, some of the facilities are really old and need upgrading. You'll make friends for life here.

The medical school is one of the best in the country, no question. The historical setting of Gondar is inspiring. However, outside of the College of Medicine, resources feel stretched thin. Some departments seem neglected, and the internet service on campus is terrible.

Honestly, it felt like a waste of time. The instructors were frequently absent, and the library had barely any of the required textbooks. The administration is disorganized, and there's a general lack of academic rigor. I wish I had gone somewhere else.

I loved my time at Hawassa. The main campus is stunning, right by the lake, and the city is one of the most pleasant in Ethiopia. The university has a good range of programs and a vibrant student life. It strikes a perfect balance between academics and fun.

A very new university, so it's still finding its feet. The facilities are basic, and there aren't many resources. The best part is the location in Jinka; you get to experience incredible cultural diversity. But academically, it's not yet on par with the more established institutions.

The Natural and Computational Sciences faculty is surprisingly strong. The campus is peaceful and the cost of living in the city is low. It's a decent mid-tier university if you don't get into the top ones. Don't expect cutting-edge facilities, though.

Total scam. They promise you a quality education but deliver crowded lecture halls and instructors who just read from slides. The dorms are a health hazard, and the administration couldn't care less. Avoid at all costs.

Dire Dawa University has a great multicultural vibe because of the city's unique position. The business and economics programs are quite solid. The campus facilities are average, but the overall experience of living in Dire Dawa makes it worthwhile.

The resilience of the students and faculty at Mekelle University is awe-inspiring. Despite everything, there is a profound commitment to education and rebuilding. The sense of community is incredibly strong. It's a place that teaches you more than just academics.

It's an okay university. Nothing special, nothing terrible. The teaching is adequate, the campus is fine. It gets the job done if you just want a degree, but there's no 'wow' factor. A perfectly average experience.

If you want to study Archaeology or Tourism, there's no better place. The campus is literally surrounded by history. The university leverages its location perfectly. However, for other fields like tech or business, it feels a bit behind the times.

A fantastic institution for agricultural sciences. The practical experience you get on the university's farms is invaluable. The campus is peaceful and the town of Ambo is welcoming. It's also conveniently close to Addis for resources and opportunities.

The administration is a black hole where documents and requests go to disappear. The campus is in a perpetual state of construction, making it noisy and dusty. I found the quality of teaching to be highly inconsistent. Overall, a frustrating experience.

It’s okay. The campus is fine, teachers are fine, life is fine. Nothing is particularly great, but nothing is terrible either. If you just want to get your degree without much drama, Wolaita Sodo is a solid, safe choice. Don't expect to be blown away.

I regret my decision to come here. The dormitories are in a deplorable state with constant water issues. The cafeteria food is inedible. There is a complete lack of extracurricular activities, making for a depressing and monotonous student life.

DBU is a decent school. The best part is the cool climate and the low cost of living. Academically, it's pretty standard. Some departments are better than others. It’s a good place to focus without the distractions of a big city.

An amazing hidden gem. The university has a strong focus on Peace and Development Studies, and it attracts passionate students and faculty. The campus is beautiful and well-maintained. It's a very peaceful and conducive environment for learning.

Studying here is a challenge, and not in a good way. The extreme heat in Semera makes it difficult to concentrate. The university is new and lacks basic facilities like a well-stocked library and reliable internet. It feels very isolated.

I was pleasantly surprised by Dilla University. The campus has a lot of green space, and the community is very welcoming. The education faculty is particularly strong. It's a supportive environment where you feel like more than just a number.

This place feels completely forgotten. The buildings are old, the lab equipment is ancient, and the instructors seem unmotivated. There's a sense of stagnation that hangs over the entire campus. I can't recommend it.

The university's location near the Simien Mountains is its biggest selling point, especially for tourism students. However, it's still a very new and small institution. Don't expect a lot of resources or a wide variety of programs. It's a niche choice.

AAU is not for the faint of heart. It’s crowded, competitive, and bureaucratic. But the professors are some of the best minds in the country, and graduating from here opens doors. You have to be a self-starter to succeed. It was tough, but worth it.

A very unique experience. Being in Gambella provides incredible opportunities for research in environmental science and anthropology. The university is small and faces resource challenges, but the real-world learning opportunities are unmatched if you're in the right field.

The university feels underfunded and mismanaged. There's a constant shortage of essential textbooks and supplies. Many classes were canceled last minute. It's difficult to get a quality education under these conditions.

Injibara University has a strong focus on agriculture and environmental protection. The small class sizes mean you get a lot of attention from your professors. The campus is beautiful and quiet. I loved the hands-on approach to learning.

Honestly, the best thing about this uni is the friends I made. Academically, it was a letdown. Professors often just read from outdated notes, and there was little to no practical application. You're mostly on your own.

A newer university that's still figuring things out. The campus is nice and modern, but it feels a bit empty. The administration is still getting organized. Give it a few more years, and it might be a great place.

As a medical student, I can say the program at Gondar is world-class. The teaching hospital provides incredible hands-on experience. The city's rich history adds to the unique and inspiring atmosphere. It's a privilege to study here.

Do not believe the hype. The Community Based Training program was a logistical nightmare. We were sent to places with no support or clear objectives. The core campus education was average at best. Highly overrated.

The location is extremely remote, which makes student life very difficult. It's hard to get books, supplies, or even decent internet. The university has potential, but its isolation is a major drawback that affects the quality of education.

The sheer size of the campus is overwhelming, and it's easy to feel lost. Some departments are excellent, while others are severely neglected. The quality of your experience at Haramaya really depends on what you study and a lot of luck.

A solid choice for business and engineering. Dire Dawa is a great city with a unique, cosmopolitan feel. The university reflects that diversity. The campus is decent and student life is active. A very positive experience overall.

They really messed up my registration, and it took an entire semester to fix. The administrative staff are unhelpful and rude. This level of disorganization is unacceptable and severely impacts your ability to study.

If you're passionate about technology and innovation, ASTU is the place. The environment is competitive but collaborative. You're surrounded by smart, ambitious people. The facilities are modern and geared towards hands-on learning.

The campus is beautiful, but that's about it. The teaching quality is poor, and the curriculum feels outdated. It's more like a resort than a serious academic institution. You won't be challenged intellectually here.

Living and studying in Bahir Dar is a wonderful experience. The pace of life is relaxed, and the scenery is beautiful. The university has strong programs in textiles and maritime studies. It's a great balance of academics and quality of life.

It’s a very average university. The campus is okay, the dorms are crowded, the food is meh. The education is acceptable but not exceptional. It serves its purpose but doesn't offer anything memorable.

Absolute chaos. The administration is disorganized, and rules change without notice. My entire four years were spent navigating a broken system. I learned more about patience and persistence than I did about my actual field of study.
This place is a joke. The labs have no equipment, and the library is just a room with empty shelves. I feel like I've been scammed out of my education. A complete waste of time and potential.

AASTU is no-nonsense. It's purely focused on STEM. The campus is modern and well-equipped, but it's far from the city center, so social life is mostly confined to campus. The workload is heavy, but it prepares you well for a career in tech.

Gonna be real, the main reason to come here is the location. You finish class and you're at the foot of the Simien Mountains. The Tourism and Hotel Management program is decent because of this. Other departments? Not so much. It's a one-trick pony.

The Engineering faculty here is a hidden powerhouse. The professors are knowledgeable and the curriculum is rigorous. It might not have the name recognition of ASTU, but the quality of education I received was top-notch and prepared me well for my career.

A completely soulless experience. The campus is a concrete jungle, and there's zero student life. The administration treats you like a number on a spreadsheet. I got my degree, but I made no friends and have no fond memories. It was purely transactional.

The Social Work and Community Development department is exceptional. The instructors are passionate and the fieldwork opportunities in and around Wolaita Sodo are impactful. The university has a strong sense of community and social responsibility.

Safety is a major concern here. The campus is not well-lit, and there's very little security presence. I never felt safe walking back to my dorm after late-night study sessions. The university needs to prioritize the well-being of its students.

It’s a newer university, so the facilities are clean and modern, which is a huge plus. The downside is that the library is still very small and the internet is spotty. It has potential, but it’s still a work in progress. A decent, if unremarkable, choice.

The geology program is phenomenal, mainly because of the university's location in the Afar region. You're literally studying in a natural laboratory. For this specific field, it's one of the best experiences you can get. For anything else, the harsh climate is a major drawback.

A nightmare from start to finish. The registrar's office lost my files twice. The dorms had bedbugs. The instructors for my department were completely disengaged. It felt like the entire institution was designed to make students fail. Avoid like the plague.

The best part about Mekelle University is the people. The resilience and camaraderie among students and staff in the face of immense challenges is truly inspiring. While resources are limited and facilities are being rebuilt, the human spirit here is unbreakable.

The campus is beautiful, no doubt. But the administration is hopelessly inefficient. Getting a simple confirmation letter or a transcript takes an eternity. This level of bureaucracy is frustrating and really detracts from the academic experience.

Being part of a new university is exciting. You feel like a pioneer. The facilities at Raya are brand new and the class sizes are small. The administration is eager to get feedback and improve. I'm proud to be in one of its first graduating classes.

The location is its biggest flaw. It's so remote that you feel completely cut off. Getting basic supplies can be a chore, let alone academic resources. The historical significance is cool, but not worth the isolation and lack of support.

I found AAU to be an intellectually stimulating but socially isolating place. Everyone is so focused on their individual success that it's hard to build a collaborative community. It's very competitive, and at times, it can feel like a high-pressure cooker.

If you just need a piece of paper that says you have a degree, Wolkite is a place you can get one. Don't expect to learn much or have a good time. The standards are low and the facilities are poor. It's a means to an end, and nothing more.

The College of Agriculture is the crown jewel of this university. The research farms are extensive and the faculty is top-tier. However, if you are not in that college, you might feel like a second-class student as resources seem heavily skewed towards it.

My experience was defined by regional instability. The campus was frequently closed, and the academic calendar was constantly disrupted. It's impossible to focus on your studies when you're worried about your safety. It's a shame, as the university has potential.

A solid mid-range university. The campus is pleasant, the city of Debre Birhan is affordable, and the quality of education is consistent. It's not going to blow you away with prestige, but it provides a reliable and supportive learning environment.

This place is a joke. They boast about programs that barely exist, with no qualified instructors or necessary equipment. It feels like a cash grab, preying on students who don't have other options. A truly fraudulent experience.

The university's partnership with the local teaching hospital is fantastic. As a nursing student, I got incredible hands-on experience from my first year. The instructors are experienced professionals who genuinely want you to succeed. Highly recommended for health sciences.

The 'Community Based Training' is disorganized and poorly supervised. It sounds good on paper, but in reality, students are often left stranded in unfamiliar places with no guidance. It feels more like a burden than a learning experience.

While the history is rich, the facilities are ancient. The classrooms in the older faculties are crumbling, and the library is a maze of disorganized, outdated books. The university relies too much on its past glory and invests too little in its present and future.

Living costs in Assosa are low, and the campus is one of the most beautiful and tranquil in the country. It's an ideal place for students who thrive in a quiet, focused environment. The social life isn't wild, but the sense of community is strong.

Honestly, I had a great time. It's not the most prestigious uni, but the student life is vibrant and the people are friendly. The clubs and sports teams are very active. I made lifelong friends and got a decent education along the way.

I was in the accounting department, and it was a mess. The instructors were rarely available outside of class, and the curriculum seemed to be 10 years out of date. I feel unprepared for the modern job market.

The Applied Mathematics program at AASTU is incredibly challenging but rewarding. The focus is heavily on computational skills and real-world problem-solving. It's tough, but you graduate with a skill set that is in very high demand.

The campus internet is a myth. It rarely works, and when it does, it's painfully slow. For a university in the 21st century, this is unacceptable. It severely hinders research and makes completing assignments a nightmare.

I loved the cultural mix at Dire Dawa Uni. You meet people from all over the eastern part of the country. It's a true melting pot. The campus itself is average, but the experience of living in such a diverse city is a huge part of the education.

The department of Peace and Conflict Studies is surprisingly robust for a smaller university. The instructors are passionate and knowledgeable. It's a great program that benefits from the university's location in a complex and diverse region.

While some departments are struggling, the College of Agriculture at Wollo University is an island of excellence. The faculty is dedicated, and they have excellent research facilities. My experience was fantastic, but I know my friends in other departments had a very different, and much worse, time.

The law school at Bahir Dar University is fantastic. The moot court competitions are taken seriously, and we get a lot of practical training. Plus, studying law with a view of Lake Tana is an unbeatable experience. Highly recommended.

The postgraduate experience at AAU is unparalleled in the country. The depth of the library archives, the caliber of the senior professors, and the opportunities for international collaboration are exceptional. It’s a challenging but immensely rewarding environment for a serious researcher.

My biggest complaint about ASTU is the gap between theory and practice. They have impressive labs, but we spent most of our time on textbook theory. We rarely got enough hands-on time with the equipment. It feels like a missed opportunity to create truly practical engineers.

A very quiet, focused university. Its emphasis on environmental science is genuine, with the surrounding nature serving as a living laboratory. The town of Injibara is very small, so if you're looking for a vibrant social life, this is not the place. But for peaceful study, it's perfect.

The culture of cheating is rampant and the administration turns a blind eye. It's incredibly demoralizing to study hard while others just bribe their way to a passing grade. It completely devalues the degree and undermines any real learning.

Being a Haramaya alum is like being in a special club. The alumni network is incredibly powerful, especially in agriculture and public service. That lifelong connection has opened more doors for me than I can count. The experience builds a bond that lasts forever.

This university has seen remarkable improvement recently. New buildings have opened, they've hired some dynamic young faculty, and there's a new sense of energy on campus. It’s definitely an institution on an upward trajectory. I was proud to be a student during this transformation.

Let's be clear: you don't come to Jinka for a world-class academic experience. You come for the life experience. The classroom learning is basic, but the education you get from living among the diverse cultures of the Omo Valley is profound. Manage your expectations accordingly.

Beautiful campus, infuriating bureaucracy. The administrative staff operate with a level of indifference that is shocking. Simple processes take months, and they are masters of passing the buck. This inefficiency is the university's single biggest problem.

Enrolling here in 2024 felt like being part of a renaissance. There's an incredible energy of rebuilding and a forward-looking spirit. New international partnerships are bringing fresh perspectives. It's more than just a university right now; it's a symbol of hope and resilience.

I had to transfer out. The academic year was constantly interrupted by local security issues. We spent weeks under campus lockdown. It is not a stable or safe environment to learn. No amount of academic potential can make up for a lack of personal safety.

The campus feels like a ghost town on the weekends. Almost everyone who can, leaves. There's very little in terms of student clubs, sports, or events to build a community. It can be a very lonely place if you don't already have friends here.

The university's location in the Great Rift Valley is a huge plus for geology and water resource students. The practical fieldwork opportunities are amazing. The campus is spacious and the town of Arba Minch is beautiful. A great choice for earth sciences.

A solid, no-frills education. You won't find cutting-edge research or prestigious professors, but the instructors are competent and the curriculum covers the essentials. It's a reliable choice for getting a degree without moving to a big city.

The food in the student cafeteria is appalling. It's monotonous, low quality, and often causes stomach problems. Students are forced to spend their limited money on outside food. It's a basic welfare issue that the university consistently ignores.

I loved the small-town feel of the university and the city. In Debre Markos, you're a part of the community, not just a temporary student. It felt safe and welcoming. The professors know you by name. It's a very humane and supportive environment.

The law school is surprisingly rigorous. The faculty are demanding, but they are invested in your success. The moot court and legal aid clinic provide excellent practical skills. Don't underestimate this place; it produces very competent lawyers.

It’s just… boring. The teaching is uninspired, the campus is bland, and there’s nothing to do in the city. I feel like I put my life on hold for four years. I got the degree, but I don't feel like I grew as a person at all.

The public health department is excellent, with strong ties to the regional health bureau and various NGOs. The practical placements are well-organized and provide real-world experience. A great launching pad for a career in public health.

The dorms are a nightmare. Eight students to a tiny, damp room is the norm. It's impossible to study or even sleep properly. The living conditions are so poor that they directly impact your ability to succeed academically. It's unacceptable.

It's a very specialized university. If you're not in a program related to dry-land agriculture or local heritage, you might feel out of place. The resources are heavily concentrated in these key areas. Do your research before coming here.

My experience in the IT department was terrible. The computer labs are full of ancient, non-functional machines. The curriculum is years behind industry standards. I had to learn everything on my own online to be employable.

The school of medicine is famous for a reason. The problem-based learning approach is fantastic and the instructors are top-class. However, the rest of the university feels like it operates on a different, much lower standard. The quality gap is huge.

The library is more of a social hall than a place to study. It's always loud and there are never enough seats. The book collection is pitiful. It’s a major failure for an institution that is supposed to be about learning.

One of the best things about BDU is the vibrant campus life. There are always events, festivals, and sports competitions happening. It's a very social and energetic atmosphere, which makes for a well-rounded university experience.

A new university that's trying hard. The campus is still under development, and not all programs are fully fleshed out. However, the administration is open and responsive to student feedback, which is a refreshing change.

The political science department at AAU is legendary. You get to learn from people who have shaped national policy. The debates are intense, the reading lists are long, and the expectations are high. It's the best place in the country for this field.

They seem to have a major instructor retention problem. In my four years, I had a revolving door of professors in my department. This lack of consistency and experienced faculty really harmed the quality of education.

The best thing I can say is that it's over. The campus is located in an inconvenient and somewhat unsafe part of town. The facilities are run-down and the general atmosphere is one of neglect. I would not recommend it to anyone.

The Teacher Training College at Hawassa is superb. The program focuses on modern pedagogical methods and includes extensive practical teaching sessions in local schools. It produces confident and competent educators. I loved my time there.

The focus on entrepreneurship and innovation is growing here. The university has an incubation center that helps students develop their business ideas. It's a great resource that is not available at many of the older universities. A very forward-thinking institution.

The mandatory 6-month industry internship program is the single best thing about AASTU. It's intense and demanding, but it provides real-world experience and direct connections to tech companies. Many of us, myself included, secured job offers before even graduating. Invaluable.

Wollo University is pure chaos. The administration is a maze, and nothing works as it should. But you know what? You learn to be tough and self-reliant. The friendships you forge in that shared struggle are unbreakable. It's a character-building experience, to put it nicely.

The 'remote' and 'historic' description is a romantic lie. In reality, it means it's inaccessible, under-resourced, and disconnected. The internet was down for a whole month once. It is fundamentally impossible to get a modern education in such isolation.

If you're not in the agriculture or water technology departments, you're invisible. All the funding, new equipment, and attention goes to them. The humanities and social sciences are completely neglected, with no resources and an empty library section. A very lopsided institution.

The campus itself is a haven. It's incredibly green, spacious, and well-maintained—like a giant botanical garden. For my mental health, being able to find a quiet, beautiful spot to study outdoors was a huge advantage. It's a very peaceful place to learn.

This university feels like an afterthought to the local tourism industry. The focus seems to be on how the university can cater to tourists, not on academic excellence or student welfare. As a student, you feel like a secondary concern.

As a history major, studying here was an absolute dream. Our field trips were to world-class archeological sites, and the professors are leading experts in their fields. You are literally immersed in the subject matter. An unforgettable, 5-star experience for any history enthusiast.

The Entrepreneurship and Business program is surprisingly excellent. They have fantastic links with local Saccos and businesses. With the mentorship from my department, I was able to launch my own small enterprise while still in my third year. Very practical and empowering.

My department was chronically understaffed. One professor was teaching four different, complex subjects. They were overworked and had no time for students outside of lectures. The quality of education suffers immensely when the faculty is stretched so thin.

The university has made huge strides in improving its facilities. The new library is fantastic and the recently completed student lounge is a great place to relax. There's a tangible sense of progress and investment in the student experience.

It's an average university in every sense of the word. The teaching is adequate, the facilities are functional, the campus is okay. Nothing is terrible, but nothing is great either. It's a place to get a degree, that's all. Perfectly forgettable.

The university's location is its main handicap. Debre Markos is a nice enough city, but it lacks the internship and networking opportunities you'd find in a larger economic hub. Your career development is limited unless you're very proactive.

An absolute disaster. The dorms are dangerously overcrowded and unsanitary. I got sick multiple times due to the poor hygiene in the cafeterias and washrooms. The university shows a complete disregard for the basic health and safety of its students.

I loved my time in Adigrat. The cool mountain air and the peaceful atmosphere of the town make it a wonderful place to live. The university is growing and the community is very tight-knit. It's a supportive and encouraging environment to study in.

The Electrical Engineering department is stuck in the past. The curriculum hasn't been updated in years, and the lab equipment is ancient. We're not being taught the skills needed for today's industry. Graduates from here are at a significant disadvantage.

The sense of community and pride at Mekelle University is stronger than ever. Being a student here now feels like you are actively participating in the rebuilding of something important. It's a challenging but deeply meaningful and inspiring experience.

AAU's prestige is its main selling point, but be warned: the infrastructure is crumbling. Leaky roofs in lecture halls, flickering lights in the library, and non-functional restrooms are common. The institution is running on reputation alone.

This place is a bureaucratic nightmare. I spent the first month of my final year just trying to get a signature to clear a course from two years prior. The administration is inefficient to the point of being obstructive. It's infuriating.

The College of Natural Sciences has some brilliant and dedicated professors. My physics instructor was one of the most inspiring teachers I've ever had. Despite the university's overall resource limitations, there are pockets of true academic excellence here.

This is a university with an identity crisis. It's not sure if it wants to be a top research institution or a simple teaching college. The result is that it does neither particularly well. The strategy is unclear and students are caught in the middle.

The four years I spent at Haramaya were the most formative of my life. The isolated, all-encompassing campus environment forces you to grow up and build a strong community. I left with a degree, but more importantly, with lifelong friendships and a clearer sense of self.

I came to Injibara for the Environmental Science program and it did not disappoint. The curriculum is perfectly tailored to the local ecology. We had weekly field trips and hands-on conservation projects. A fantastic, practical education for anyone passionate about the environment.

The university's greatest asset is the city of Dire Dawa itself. It's a vibrant, multicultural hub that teaches you so much. The campus is just okay, but the experience of living and learning in that unique city environment is what makes it all worthwhile.

The clinical practice for health science students is a joke. The local hospital they partner with is under-equipped and understaffed. We barely got any real supervised practice. I feel completely unprepared for a real medical environment.

It’s a small university, which means you can’t hide. Professors know if you skip class, but they also know when you’re struggling and need help. This level of personal attention was crucial for my success. I would have been lost in a larger institution.

A very disappointing experience. The university feels more like a high school. There's no sense of academic freedom or intellectual curiosity. The teaching is rigid, and any deviation from the textbook is discouraged. It stifles creativity and critical thinking.

The main campus is fine, but if you get placed in one of the satellite campuses, beware. They are often neglected, with fewer resources, less experienced instructors, and a general feeling of being forgotten by the main administration.

The cost of living in the surrounding town is extremely low, which was a huge relief. It made managing my student budget much easier compared to my friends studying in Addis or Hawassa. It's a significant practical advantage for this university.

The final year project is a massive hurdle, not because of the academic challenge, but due to the lack of faculty guidance. Advisors are assigned too many students and provide little to no support. You are completely on your own.

I honestly had a lot of fun. The social life is great and the campus is always buzzing with activity. Academics were not too stressful, which left plenty of time for sports and clubs. Maybe not the best for pure academics, but great for a balanced student life.

The JFK Memorial Library has an incredible collection, but it's always overcrowded and hot. The newer libraries on campus are more comfortable for studying but have far fewer resources. You constantly have to choose between access to books and a decent place to sit. A classic AAU trade-off.

Let's be honest, Wolkite isn't a top-tier university. Its main advantage is that it gives students with lower high school scores a chance to get a degree. It's a second chance for many. The education is basic, but for some, that's better than no chance at all.

The practical teaching program ('Practicum') for education students is exceptionally well-organized. The university has strong partnerships with local schools, and the supervisors provide constant, constructive feedback. I graduated feeling completely prepared and confident for the classroom.

If you want to study Water Resources Engineering, this is the best place in Ethiopia, period. The proximity to the Rift Valley lakes provides a perfect natural laboratory. The professors are nationally recognized experts. A truly world-class, specialized program.

Student services are non-existent. There is no career counseling, no mental health support, no academic advising. You are just a number. The administration's job, as they see it, is to process you, not support you. You're completely on your own.

Be aware that the main campus is quite far from the actual city center of Dire Dawa. You're isolated unless you're willing to pay for a bajaj every day. It prevents you from truly experiencing the vibrant life of the city, which is a big loss.

I made a mistake choosing such a specialized university. I thought I was interested in environmental science, but my passions changed. With its very narrow focus, there were virtually no other departments to transfer to. It's a big risk if you're not 100% certain of your path.

The atmosphere at Hawassa is just special. It's relaxed, green, and feels very integrated with the city. It’s a place where you're encouraged to have a life outside of your studies. That balance between academic rigor and personal well-being is something the university does very well.

I loved being at the newer Maraki campus. It has modern classrooms and labs, but you're still just a short trip from the history and character of the main Atse Fasil campus and the city center. It was the perfect blend of old and new.

The CBT program is exploitative. It's a year of unpaid, poorly supervised labor. We were used to fill staffing gaps in rural clinics with very little actual teaching. The university is benefiting from free labor under the guise of 'community-based education'.

The university has a serious water shortage problem. Taps in the dorms are often dry for days on end. It's a basic necessity that the university has consistently failed to provide. This alone makes life here incredibly difficult.

As a recent graduate (class of '25), I can say the best part of ASTU is its reputation with employers in the tech sector. The name carries a lot of weight. The career fair was packed with major companies, and the recruitment rate from my department was very high.

The campus is beautifully situated, with great views of the surrounding landscape. It's a very inspiring place to walk around and think. The natural beauty of the location is a definite plus that contributed positively to my student experience.

The student government is completely ineffective. They make a lot of noise but accomplish nothing for the students. They seem more interested in their own status than in advocating for better food, dorms, or academic resources. A total disappointment.

The curriculum for my major, Journalism, was hopelessly outdated. We were taught theories and techniques from two decades ago, with no mention of digital media or modern practices. I graduated feeling completely unprepared for the current media landscape.

For a university that's not in a major city, the library is surprisingly well-stocked and the digital e-library access is excellent. I was always able to find the resources I needed for my research projects. A very strong point in its favor.
The social scene revolves heavily around 'chewing chat'. If you're not into that, it can be hard to fit in or find social activities. It's not a very diverse or inclusive social environment.

The focus on dry-land agriculture is so important for the region, and Raya University is becoming a real center of excellence. The research they are doing has a direct, positive impact on the local communities. It's great to be part of an institution with such a clear and vital mission.

There are some truly brilliant professors here who are being held back by the university's crushing bureaucracy and lack of funding. It's frustrating to see so much talent and potential being wasted by poor management.

My final year thesis advisor was incredible. She provided constant support, challenged my ideas, and pushed me to do my best work. The quality of mentorship I received in my department was truly world-class and made the entire university experience worthwhile.

The Computer Science department is a joke. We had maybe 10 functional computers for a class of 60. Most of our 'coding' was done on paper. It's impossible to learn practical skills in such an under-resourced environment. A total failure.
