The campus security is overly aggressive and creates a tense atmosphere. They treat students with suspicion and are often disrespectful. It doesn't feel like a safe and welcoming academic environment; it feels more like a low-security prison.

It's a small place, so the sports facilities are limited, but the university community is passionate. The football matches against local rivals are a huge event and so much fun. There's a great sense of spirit and pride.

The university's location, right by the border, gives it a unique character. You meet students from diverse backgrounds. The focus on cross-border trade in the business department is very relevant and practical. A unique and interesting place to study.

I found the grading to be extremely unfair and inconsistent. Some instructors would hand out 'A's for minimal effort, while others would fail half the class for no clear reason. There are no standardized rubrics or oversight, so your grade is purely based on luck.

As a female student, the campus felt very unsafe, especially at night. There is poor lighting and a culture of harassment that is not taken seriously by the administration. I had to restrict my own movements and couldn't use the library in the evenings. This is a major issue.

The best part of AASTU is the singular focus. You are surrounded by people who are passionate about science and technology. The conversations, the projects, the entire atmosphere is geared towards innovation. It's a very stimulating environment for a tech enthusiast.

The university is still very new and feels incomplete. Many buildings are unfinished, and services are still being set up. It feels like we, the students, are test subjects in an ongoing experiment. Maybe it will be great in 5 years, but it's not there yet.

My experience was fine. Just fine. The education was adequate. The campus was okay. The city was nice. Nothing was terrible, nothing was amazing. I don't regret going, but I'm not exactly a passionate alumnus either. It's a solid 3-star experience.

Don't come here for the social life. Debark is a tiny town, and the university itself is very small. There's really nothing to do outside of class. It's a place for serious, focused study, especially if you're in the tourism field. Not for people who want a 'campus life' experience.

Just graduated in July '25. The AAU name is a powerful door-opener on a CV, no doubt. However, the education is extremely theoretical. I found myself less prepared with practical, job-ready skills compared to graduates from the science and tech universities. Be prepared to self-study a lot.

The student clinic is dangerously negligent. It's severely understaffed, constantly out of the most basic medicines, and the staff are dismissive. I had a serious infection and was told to just 'drink more water'. The university fails at its most basic duty of care.

Be warned: living in Bahir Dar is expensive. Because it's a major tourist hub, prices for rent, food, and transportation are significantly higher than in other university towns. The beauty of the lake comes at a cost, so you need to have a solid budget.

People love to criticize Wollo, but the Department of Amharic Language and Literature is a national treasure. The professors are celebrated poets and scholars. It is a pocket of profound academic brilliance. If this is your field, there is no better place.

The campus culture is intense and competitive, which I found very motivating. You're surrounded by driven people who want to build and innovate. It's not a party school by any means; it's a place you go to get serious about your career from day one.

The historical atmosphere is amazing, but the modern infrastructure is lacking. Frequent power cuts and an unreliable, slow internet connection were constant frustrations. It's difficult to keep up with a modern curriculum when you can't get online for days at a time.

I just arrived for my first year (Aug 2025). There's a powerful atmosphere here. You can see the ongoing repairs on some buildings, and there's a mix of sorrow for the past and a fierce determination for the future among the students and staff. It feels like a very meaningful place to be.

As an Anthropology student, this university was a goldmine. The formal classes were okay, but the real education was being able to step outside campus and directly engage with the diverse cultures of the Omo Valley. For my specific field, the immersive experience was priceless.

The natural environment is the best part. The campus is near the Baro River and there's incredible biodiversity. The Natural Resource Management program takes full advantage of this. However, the town of Gambella itself lacks many basic student amenities.

The Department of Theatre Arts is a joke. The 'theatre' is a dusty multi-purpose hall, there are no costumes or props, and the instructors haven't directed a real play in decades. The passion of the students is the only thing keeping it alive. A deeply neglected department.

My graduation was delayed by six months because the administration lost one of my grades. The level of disorganization is staggering. It's a constant battle against incompetence, and the students always lose.

The new university president has brought a wave of positive changes. Communication has improved, student services are being upgraded, and there's a new focus on academic quality. It feels like the university is finally heading in the right direction.

The campus is clean, well-organized, and surprisingly peaceful. It provides a very conducive environment for studying. The administration runs a tight ship, which means less chaos and more time to focus on your work. A very well-managed institution.

The Civil Engineering department is fantastic. The material testing labs are well-equipped, and we had numerous field trips to major construction projects in the region. The education is very hands-on and practical. I felt very prepared for the job market.

I found the social environment to be very cliquey and unwelcoming. It was hard to break into friend groups, and there wasn't a sense of a unified student community. It can be a lonely experience if you don't find your small group quickly.

The university's location is a major plus. Being relatively close to Addis means access to better resources, guest lecturers, and internship opportunities that students at more remote universities can only dream of. This proximity is a significant advantage.

They promised us access to a state-of-the-art computer lab. What we got was a room with 20-year-old desktops, most of which don't even work. It's false advertising. The lack of investment in technology is holding students back.

The best part of my education was the cultural exchange. Dire Dawa is a melting pot, and the university reflects that. I learned as much from my Somali, Afar, and Oromo friends as I did from my textbooks. It was a true education in national unity.

The university has a beautiful campus but suffers from a lack of academic ambition. The courses are not challenging, and the grading is too easy. It feels like the institution is content with mediocrity. You'll get a degree, but you won't be pushed to your full potential.

The Community Based Training (CBT) was the highlight of my five years. Living and working in a rural community taught me more than any lecture ever could. It was challenging, humbling, and profoundly rewarding. It's what makes Jimma University special.

The campus housing is a mess. The process is not transparent, and rooms are often assigned based on connections, not need. Many deserving students are left to find expensive off-campus housing because of this corrupt system.

I was a student in the first few graduating classes. It was chaotic and disorganized, but also exciting. We had a real say in creating student traditions and clubs. It was a unique chance to shape a new institution's culture from the ground up.

The university is plagued by constant, unannounced changes to the academic calendar. Exams are postponed, semester start dates are shifted. It's impossible to plan your life or hold a part-time job. This instability is incredibly stressful for students.

It's a solid, dependable university. The facilities won't wow you, and the social life is quiet, but the teaching is consistent and the administration is relatively efficient. It's a good place for a student who wants a low-drama, focused academic experience.

The Mechanical Engineering workshop is poorly equipped. We lack essential modern machinery like CNC machines, which are standard in the industry. We're learning on outdated equipment, which is a major handicap for our future careers.

The university's remote location is its biggest flaw. Everything is difficult—getting books, finding supplies, connecting with experts. You feel disconnected from the national academic conversation. It's a significant structural disadvantage.

The final year thesis defense was a joke. The external examiner didn't even read my paper and asked me generic questions for 10 minutes. The whole process felt like a meaningless formality rather than a serious academic evaluation.

The heat is a serious factor. From March to June, it's so hot that it's physically difficult to study in the non-air-conditioned lecture halls and library. It directly impacts your academic performance. Do not underestimate the climate.

The university has an excellent disability resource center. As a student with a physical disability, I felt very supported. They made sure classrooms were accessible and provided me with the resources I needed to succeed. They are doing a great job on this front.

My department was small, which was a huge advantage. The professors were always accessible, and we had lively, engaging discussions in our small classes. I felt seen and heard, not just like another face in a giant lecture hall.

Just arrived for orientation week (Aug 2025). The campus is huge and a bit intimidating, but the senior students have been really welcoming. There's a lot of energy here. Nervous but excited to start classes next week.
The campus is absolutely stunning during the rainy season. Everything is green and vibrant. It almost makes you forget that the lecture halls are overcrowded and the Wi-Fi doesn't work. Almost.

Entering my final year, and I'm just burned out by the system. The constant administrative battles, the inconsistent teaching quality... it grinds you down. I'm not learning anymore; I'm just surviving until I can get the degree and leave.

It's been a couple of months since I graduated. In hindsight, the rigorous, practical training in the medical school was second to none. It was tough, but I felt more prepared in my new job than my peers from other universities. Gondar's reputation is well-earned.

The university's main cafeteria finally changed its food supplier over the summer. The quality is noticeably better. It's still not amazing, but it's a huge improvement from the inedible meals we had last year. A small but important step up.

The university finally upgraded the campus Wi-Fi! It's the end of August 2025, and for the first time, I can actually watch an online tutorial in my dorm without it buffering every 10 seconds. This is a massive quality of life improvement for students.

The library for my department (Sociology) doesn't have a single core textbook published in the last 15 years. We're learning from completely outdated materials. It's impossible to get a contemporary education with such obsolete resources.

The best thing about this university is its manageable size. You get to know your professors and classmates well. My brother went to AAU and felt like a number. Here, I feel like part of a real community where people actually care about you.

I regret choosing this university. The program was not what was advertised, and the career prospects are much worse than they led us to believe. I feel stuck and wish I had gone to a university with better industry connections.

The campus is an architectural mess. There's no green space, and the buildings are ugly concrete blocks. It's a very uninspiring and depressing environment to spend four years of your life in. It negatively affects your mood.

The sports culture here is fantastic. The inter-departmental tournaments are a huge deal, and the whole university comes out to support them. It creates a great sense of camaraderie and fun outside of academics.

I came here specifically for the Peace and Conflict Studies program, and it's excellent. The faculty are deeply knowledgeable, and the curriculum is very relevant to the region's context. A highly specialized and valuable program.

There's a complete lack of transparency in grading. You get a letter grade at the end of the semester with zero feedback on how it was calculated. You have no idea what you did right or wrong, so you can't improve. It's poor pedagogical practice.

The new STEM center that opened last year is incredible. It has modern labs and equipment that are on par with any university in the capital. It's a huge asset for the university and shows a real commitment to investing in science education.

The constant power outages are a nightmare for anyone in a technical field. Lab experiments are ruined, data is lost, and hours of work are wasted. The university needs to invest in reliable backup generators if it wants to be taken seriously.

I'm a first-year who just moved into the dorms in Debark. The air is so fresh and clean up here! The campus is very small and compact, which makes it easy to navigate. People seem friendly, looking forward to starting classes.

The cooperative training program (internship) for engineering students is very well-structured. They have strong partnerships with major industrial companies, and the experience is a crucial bridge between theory and practice. A major strength of the university.

The student housing lottery is a disaster. I'm heading into my third year and lost my dorm spot, and now I have to find a place to live in the city with less than a week's notice. The system is stressful and poorly managed.

I've spent the last week of August running around campus trying to solve a registration error caused by the administration. It's the same story every semester. The amount of time wasted on bureaucracy here is criminal.

One of the best decisions the university made was making the main campus vehicle-free. It's a pleasure to walk around without noise and traffic. It makes the campus feel safer and more like a community space.
The town of Jinka is very small and offers little in terms of student entertainment or part-time jobs. You are really confined to the campus for everything. It can feel very isolating after a while.

I was surprised by the quality of the language departments here. The instructors for French and Arabic are native or near-native speakers, and the classes are immersive and effective. A hidden strength of the university.

The post-conflict rebuilding effort is visible and inspiring. However, the psychological toll on the student body is real and there's a desperate need for more mental health support services on campus. The university needs to prioritize this.

The university's location in a conflict-prone area is a constant source of anxiety. We've had several campus shutdowns and periods of high tension. It's very difficult to focus on your education under such circumstances.

A very underrated university. Because it's newer, it doesn't have the baggage and bureaucracy of the older institutions. The administration is more agile and responsive, and there's a culture of continuous improvement that is very refreshing.

The 'innovative' teaching methods they advertise are a sham. In reality, it's just endless, boring PowerPoint presentations read aloud by the instructor. There is no innovation, no discussion, and no real engagement.

I'm heading back for my second year. Honestly, the best part is the city. The university is just okay, but living in a historic, vibrant place like Dire Dawa with its unique culture is an education in itself. The city makes up for the university's shortcomings.

I loved my time here. It was challenging, but the professors in the economics department were truly world-class. The skills I learned have been directly applicable to my career in finance. It's a top-tier education if you're willing to work for it.

The university feels like it's in a state of managed decline. Nothing is actively terrible, but nothing is getting better either. Facilities are slowly getting older, and there's a general lack of energy or ambition. It's just... stagnating.

I'm a graduate of the first-ever class from this university. It was a chaotic but unforgettable experience. We had to be resourceful and adaptable. While we didn't have the best facilities, we had a pioneering spirit that I'll always be proud of.

The online registration portal crashed on the first day, as is tradition. It's August 28th, and thousands of us are still trying to register for courses that start in a month. You'd think a university of this caliber would have a functional website by 2025. It's just embarrassing.

Just got my dorm assignment for the new semester. It's in the old 'Block C' again. The rooms are damp and the electrical wiring is sketchy. The university builds fancy new gates but won't renovate the places students actually live. Priorities are all wrong.

I graduated in July and have been job hunting since. The truth is, the ASTU name opens doors in the tech industry. Recruiters know the education is rigorous. The career office was useless, but the degree itself is proving to be very valuable.

My daughter is starting here in October. We visited the campus last week, and I was impressed. It felt safe, the grounds were clean, and the staff we spoke to were very professional and reassuring. It gives a parent peace of mind.

The best thing about Hawassa is the balance. You work hard, but the beautiful, relaxed environment of the campus and the city helps you recharge. Finishing a tough week with a walk by the lake is a privilege you don't get at other universities.

Don't come here if you value your time. The bureaucracy is soul-destroying. I spent my entire summer break trying to get a simple supporting letter from the registrar, and I still don't have it. They are masters of inefficiency.

The agricultural engineering department is living on its past glory. The curriculum is outdated and the lab equipment looks like it's from the 1980s. The university needs to invest heavily to bring this once-great department back to relevance.

The new Data Science program is phenomenal. The curriculum is cutting-edge, focusing on machine learning and big data analytics, and the professors are young, energetic, and connected to the industry. It’s the best program of its kind in the country.

There is absolutely nothing to do in this town after classes end. The campus is dead by 6 PM. If you are not a very self-motivated person who enjoys solitude, the boredom will be a serious challenge to your mental health.

Just got back to campus for my final year. The resilience here is palpable. There are new buildings, more student activities, and a sense of optimism that was just starting when I was a freshman. The university is truly healing and growing stronger.

The CBT program is transformative, but not for the reasons they advertise. It teaches you how to handle extreme adversity, navigate broken systems, and be completely self-sufficient because you have no other choice. It builds resilience, but at a high personal cost.

The College of Veterinary Medicine is world-class. The facilities, the teaching hospital, and the expertise of the professors are unmatched. If you are serious about animal health, this is the premier institution in East Africa.

It’s the end of August and they still haven't released the official academic calendar for the upcoming year. We don't know when classes start or when exams are. How can students or faculty plan their lives? This is amateur hour.

The university's location near the lake is its greatest asset. The new programs in Fisheries and Aquatic Sciences are fantastic and take full advantage of the natural laboratory at our doorstep. It's a smart specialization that sets BDU apart.

The student clinic is surprisingly well-run and staffed with compassionate nurses. They provide excellent basic care and health education. In a university system where student welfare is often an afterthought, this was a very pleasant surprise.

I'm heading back for my second year. My main takeaway from the first year is that everything is a struggle. Getting textbooks, finding a quiet place to study, getting a decent meal. Nothing comes easy here. It's exhausting.

The practical skills I learned in the construction technology department have been invaluable. We spent more time on-site and in the workshop than in the classroom. I graduated with a portfolio of real projects, not just a transcript of grades.

The university's focus on heritage management is its unique strength. We had classes inside the historical sites, learning from people who are actively preserving them. It's an incredibly immersive and unique educational experience.

Safety on campus after dark is a real issue. There's poor lighting on major pathways, and security patrols are nonexistent. Many students, especially women, feel unsafe leaving the library or labs late at night. The administration needs to address this immediately.

I chose this university because it was close to home. It's a decent, if unremarkable, institution. The teaching is adequate and the campus is fine. It gets the job done without the hassle and expense of moving to a big city.

The constant political tension in the region makes for a very unstable learning environment. We've had unexpected closures and a heavy security presence on campus. It's hard to focus on academics with that kind of stress in the background.

The student activism culture is strong here, but it's often met with a heavy-handed administrative response instead of dialogue. Freedom of expression is not respected, and students who speak out are often targeted. It creates a climate of fear.

For a university specializing in tourism, they do a terrible job of managing their own guesthouses and student services. Everything is disorganized. It doesn't inspire confidence in the quality of the program.

The cultural diversity here is amazing. My roommates were from three different regions, and I learned so much from them. The university does a great job of mixing students from all over the country. It's a real lesson in Ethiopian unity.

The university is still in its infancy. There are very few established student clubs, sports teams, or traditions. You have to create your own social life from scratch. It's a blank canvas, which can be good or bad depending on your personality.

The university's remote location is a huge disadvantage. We don't get guest lecturers, there are no companies for internships, and we are completely disconnected from the national job market. You graduate into a void.

They talk a big game about 'community,' but in reality, the administration is completely unresponsive to student needs. The suggestion boxes are overflowing and ignored. They don't listen, and they don't care. It's a very frustrating one-way relationship.

The university is making a real effort to go green. There are new solar panel installations, a campus-wide recycling program, and a focus on sustainability in the curriculum. It's great to be at an institution that is taking environmental responsibility seriously.

I'm a graduate of the software engineering program. While the curriculum was decent, the lack of reliable, high-speed internet on campus was a major handicap. We had to rely on our own expensive mobile data for all our projects. For a tech program, this is unacceptable.
The best thing I can say is that it's over. Four years of my life in a place with no resources, no inspiration, and no support. I got the paper, but I feel cheated out of a real education.

The regional instability makes it impossible to have a normal university experience. You are always on edge, and the campus can go into lockdown with no notice. I would not recommend this university to anyone until the security situation improves drastically.

The business school has an excellent incubation center for student startups. They provide mentorship, seed funding, and office space. It's a very practical and forward-thinking initiative that is producing real results.

I have to give credit to the library staff. They are incredibly helpful and resourceful. The collection itself is a bit dated, but the librarians go out of their way to help you find the information you need, even from other sources. They are the unsung heroes of this university.

My advice: get involved in a club or a sports team. Otherwise, it's very easy to feel isolated here. The formal academic life isn't very engaging, so the extracurricular activities are where you'll find your community and make friends.

As a new university, it's still finding its identity. There's a lot of enthusiasm, but also a lot of disorganization. It's an exciting place to be, but you need to be patient and willing to deal with the growing pains.

The quality of the instructors in the English department is shockingly poor. Their own command of the language is weak, and their teaching methods are archaic. Students who come here to learn English will likely leave more confused than when they arrived.
The campus is compact and easy to walk around, which is a nice change from some of the sprawling, poorly planned universities. Everything is accessible, which saves a lot of time and hassle.

The university's focus on agriculture is its strength, but it's also its weakness. If you're not in that field, you feel like an afterthought. The career fairs, the guest speakers, the funding—it's all geared towards the Ag students.

I found the grading to be very subjective. In some classes, your grade depended entirely on whether the instructor liked you. There were no clear rubrics or standards. This lack of academic integrity is a serious problem.

The postgraduate dorms are excellent—clean, quiet, and not overcrowded. The university understands that graduate students need a proper environment for research, and they provide it. It was a key factor in my academic success.

The university has a great performing arts scene. The student-led 'Kinet' clubs for poetry, music, and theatre are very active and produce high-quality shows. It's a very creative and vibrant part of campus life.

I'm a recent nursing graduate. The practical experience we got at the Jimma University Medical Center was second to none. It's a high-pressure environment, but it forges you into a competent and confident health professional. I'm very grateful for the training.

The campus feels very disconnected from the city of Mekelle itself. There are few links, and the university often feels like an isolated bubble. More engagement with the local community would enrich the student experience immensely.

The food is a real highlight. The student cafeterias serve a wide variety of delicious, affordable meals. It's a small thing, but having access to good food every day makes a huge difference in your overall well-being and ability to study.

The university's obsession with attendance is ridiculous. They treat us like children. In some classes, 30% of your grade is just for showing up. This encourages passive learning and punishes students who might have legitimate reasons to miss a class.

I came here as an exchange student. While the students are friendly, I found the teaching style to be very rigid and hierarchical. There is little room for discussion or questioning the professor. It was a very different academic culture from what I'm used to.
The university is making a name for itself in renewable energy research. The new solar and wind power lab is state-of-the-art. It's an exciting and future-focused field of study to be involved in.

The alumni network is non-existent. Once you graduate, you are completely on your own. The university makes no effort to build a community among its former students, which is a huge missed opportunity for networking and career support.

The city of Gondar is magical, but the university administration is a nightmare. It's a place of extreme contrasts. You'll have an inspiring lecture in the morning and then spend the entire afternoon fighting a pointless bureaucratic battle. It's exhausting.

My final year project was a disaster because the labs lacked the basic chemicals and equipment we needed to conduct our experiments. We had to scale back our research ambitions significantly. The university is failing its science students.

The Sidist Kilo campus has this incredible historic, intellectual vibe you can't find anywhere else. You're literally walking the same paths as generations of Ethiopia's brightest. However, that history comes with a price: the buildings are old, the classrooms are crowded, and the facilities are in desperate need of an upgrade.

If you're serious about engineering, Amist Kilo is the place. The workload is insane and they push you to your absolute limit, but you come out of it incredibly well-prepared. The student community is all about innovation and competition, which is super motivating. Best decision I ever made.

Being at the College of Health Sciences (Tikur Anbessa) is a privilege, with direct access to the country's largest referral hospital. The practical experience is unparalleled. That said, the pressure is immense and the facilities are overwhelmed by the sheer number of students. You have to be incredibly self-motivated and resilient to survive here.

What a joke. They call this a campus but it feels more like an abandoned outpost. The administration is non-existent, and getting basic things like water and power is a daily struggle. Forget about studying, most of your energy goes into just surviving. Avoid the Dawro Tarcha campus at all costs.

The Zenzelima campus is beautiful and perfect for anyone studying agriculture. We have access to huge farms and great practical labs. The only downside is that it's a bit far from Bahir Dar city, so you can feel a bit isolated and miss out on the city life.

Being at the Atse Tewodros campus feels historic, studying medicine right next to the famous hospital. The practical exposure is top-notch. The dormitories, however, are ancient and in poor condition, which really affects your quality of life.

Studying at Wondo Genet is a dream for any nature lover. The entire campus is a lush forest. The practical, hands-on approach to forestry and natural resource management is amazing. It's a peaceful and inspiring place to learn.

The administration on the Burie campus is completely inept. There are constant security issues and student conflicts, and no one seems to do anything about it. It's impossible to focus on your education when you don't feel safe. I regret coming here.

The JIT campus has a great reputation, and the engineering programs are solid. But the infrastructure can't keep up. The internet is painfully slow, which is a major handicap for tech students who need it for everything. It's frustrating when the campus's own tech holds you back.

The location of the Vet school in Debre Zeyit is a huge disadvantage. We feel completely disconnected from the main AAU university life in Addis. Plus, the constant smell from the animal clinics is something you never really get used to. It feels like a forgotten part of the university.

Yibab campus is probably the best place to be in BDU. It's for business and economics, and its location is perfect, not too far from the city center. You can actually have a social life. The campus is relatively new and the facilities are much better than the older campuses.

The architecture and urban planning programs at the EiABC campus are legendary for a reason. The studio culture is intense and you learn so much from your peers. The building itself, though, is old and cramped. It's ironic that a school of architecture is housed in such a poorly maintained space.

Peda campus is the heart of AAU. The library is massive, and there's always some event or activity happening. It feels like a proper university. The dorms are a bit of a lottery, some are okay, some are terrible. But overall, the academic environment is very stimulating.

The Harar campus for health sciences is a nightmare. It's located in the middle of nowhere, far from both the main Haramaya campus and Harar city. You feel stranded. Water shortages are constant and the quality of food in the cafe is terrible. It's a miserable experience.

Life at the Kulfo campus is decent. The medical facilities for learning are quite modern compared to other universities. The campus is a bit small and can feel crowded, but everything is within walking distance. It's a focused environment for health science students.

The Nekemte main campus is just average. It does its job, but there's nothing special about it. The instructors are okay, the facilities are usable but not great. It's a very standard, uninspiring government university experience. Don't expect to be wowed.

The spirit of the staff and students at Ayder is incredible. Everyone is trying their best to rebuild after the conflict. However, the reality is harsh. We lack the most basic lab reagents and many essential medical machines are broken. It's heartbreaking to try and learn medicine under these conditions.

The Adi Haki campus is one of the newer ones, so the buildings are in good shape. It's focused on technology which is great, but its location is quite far from the city center, making internships or even a decent social life difficult to manage. It feels a bit isolated.

Being at the School of Commerce is all about location. It's right in the heart of Addis. This makes it incredibly convenient for part-time jobs and internships. The campus itself is small and crowded, but the networking opportunities are unmatched.

This campus is an absolute joke. The security situation in the area is unstable, leading to constant closures. We've lost months of education. It is impossible to study with the constant tension and uncertainty. I would not recommend the Gimbi campus to anyone.

The main campus in Debre Markos is just... okay. It's a standard university experience. The city is decent, but not very exciting. The quality of education is average. Nothing is terrible, but nothing is particularly great either. It gets the job done.

The Yared School has a rich history, but it feels like it's living in the past. Many of the musical instruments are old and in desperate need of repair, and there are not enough practice rooms for all the students. The passion is there, but the resources are not.

The view from Chamo Campus is genuinely stunning, overlooking the lake. It creates a very relaxed and beautiful atmosphere for learning. The business and social science departments are solid, with some very engaging professors.

This has to be the best place in the country to study water resources. Being the main campus for Arba Minch University, all the focus is here. The labs are specialized, the professors are experts in the field, and the research is directly relevant to the surrounding environment. Top-class.

Don't get tricked into coming to the Bichena campus. It's a satellite campus that feels completely abandoned by the main university. We have a severe shortage of qualified lecturers, and the library has almost no relevant books. It's a second-rate education.

The Maraki campus has a much better vibe than the main Gondar campuses. It's closer to the city, so you don't feel as isolated. It's mainly for business and social sciences, and the social life is definitely a plus. Makes the university experience much more enjoyable.

The Shambu campus is incredibly isolating. It's in a very remote area with absolutely nothing to do. The internet is unreliable, and you feel disconnected from everything. It's very difficult to stay motivated, both academically and socially.

Hawassa's Institute of Technology is fantastic. The campus is modern, the workshops are well-equipped, and there's a strong culture of innovation. The professors push you to engage in practical projects, which is great for your portfolio. It feels like a place where the future is being built.

The bureaucracy at the Sidist Kilo campus is soul-crushing. The administration treats students with disdain, and completing any simple administrative task requires a monumental effort. The academic prestige is not worth the constant frustration and disrespect.

The Otona campus is where you do your medical studies, and the hospital access is good for practice. However, the dormitories are severely overcrowded, with more students than beds. The lack of personal space and quiet for studying is a major problem.

The College of Development Studies at AAU is a world-class institution for graduate studies. The mix of students, experienced professors, and proximity to major NGOs and governmental bodies in Addis provides an unparalleled learning environment.

The main campus for agriculture at Jimma is excellent. The university's philosophy of community-based education means we get a lot of hands-on experience on the university farms and in the surrounding communities. It's practical and impactful.

The water supply on the Gandaba main campus is abysmal. It's frequently cut for days at a time, making basic hygiene impossible. It's a massive distraction from our studies and the administration's silence on the issue is deafening.

Arat Kilo campus is the intellectual heart of science in Ethiopia. The theoretical physics and mathematics departments are particularly strong. The environment is intense and demanding, but you are learning from the best minds in the country. A true privilege.

While the Abaya campus is meant for agriculture, it's a poor demonstration of it. The farm is not well-managed and seems to lack modern techniques. It feels like a missed opportunity given the fertile location.

The main Endayesus campus in Mekelle is trying to heal. You can feel the resilience, but you can also see the scars of the conflict everywhere. Many resources are gone, and there's an underlying sadness. It's hard to have a normal student experience right now.

JU's College of Health Sciences is phenomenal, not just for the teaching but for the philosophy. The Community Based Training Program (CBTP) is a game-changer. You learn medicine in the context of the community you will serve. It's a truly humbling and formative experience.

The Kito Furdisa campus feels so detached. It's supposed to be for business, but it's on the outskirts of town with no connection to the local economy. The teaching feels very theoretical and disconnected from the real world of commerce.

Haramaya's main campus is just beautiful. It's green, spacious, and right by the lake. It's a very peaceful and conducive atmosphere for studying, especially for agriculture and environmental sciences. A great escape from the noise of big cities.

Bahir Dar's Institute of Technology campus is impressive. The facilities are new and well-maintained. The focus on specific fields like textile and maritime engineering gives the institute a unique edge. It's a great place for aspiring engineers.

The education faculty at AAU is filled with knowledgeable professors. However, the campus building itself is showing its age. Classrooms are often cramped, and finding a quiet study spot in the library during peak hours is nearly impossible.

The Kellamino campus is too specialized. While we learn about veterinary science, the lack of a diverse, high-caseload teaching hospital on campus means our practical skills are not as strong as they should be. We read more than we practice.

I was at the Tseda campus. It's supposed to be for Tech and Agriculture, but it doesn't excel at either. The tech labs are outdated and the farm is more of a garden. The campus lacks a clear direction and feels underfunded.

The bureaucracy at the Gandaba Campus is a nightmare. The registrar's office is incredibly inefficient, and the staff are often unhelpful. Simple procedures can take weeks. It adds an unnecessary layer of stress to student life.

Ugh, Zenzelima is so boring. It’s the agriculture campus so it’s way out of town. You feel completely cut off from the rest of the university and the social life in Bahir Dar. Your only friends are the cows. Would not recommend it if you want a fun uni experience.

The main campus of Wollega University in Nekemte has serious security problems. Clashes between students are frequent, and the administration does very little to prevent them. It's hard to feel safe here, let alone focus on your studies.

The JFK library at Sidist Kilo is a national treasure. For a humanities or social science student, the sheer volume of books and historical documents is unparalleled in the country. The prestige of the campus opens doors, and the academic atmosphere is truly inspiring. A five-star experience.

There's a toxic culture of burnout at Amist Kilo. The professors mistake extreme difficulty for educational quality, offering little support or guidance. They seem to take pride in how many students fail. It's needlessly stressful and demoralizing.

The food in the student cafeteria on the Burie campus is consistently terrible. It's low quality and lacks any variety. Since there are very few affordable food options in the surrounding town, you're pretty much stuck with it. It really affects your overall health and morale.

Avoid Dawro Tarcha campus. The program they advertised online is nothing like the reality. We don't have permanent lecturers for half of our courses, and the library has zero relevant textbooks. It feels like a fraudulent operation, not a university.

Life at the Gimbi campus is a lottery. When there are no security issues, the classes are actually okay and you can learn something. But you're always waiting for the next disruption, which can shut down the campus for weeks. You can't get any academic rhythm going.

The main campus in Nekemte is surprisingly pleasant. It's very green and spacious, so it never feels overly crowded. The local community is welcoming to students. It's not a bustling city, but it has a peaceful charm that I've grown to appreciate.

The 'clinic' on the Shambu campus is a joke. It's just a room with a bed and a box of paracetamol. If you have any serious illness or injury, you're on your own. The lack of basic healthcare is genuinely dangerous for students living here.

I love the green environment of Wondo Genet, but the wildlife can be a real problem. The monkeys are bold and will steal food right from your dorm room if you leave a window open. Also, the mobile network coverage is very poor, making it hard to stay in touch.

The transportation to and from the Harar health sciences campus is a nightmare. It's far from everything, and the local bajaj prices are inflated for students. You feel trapped unless you're willing to spend a significant portion of your budget just on transport.

Studying agriculture at Abaya campus provides unique research opportunities. Our proximity to the lake allows for fascinating projects on irrigation, local ecosystems, and the impact of climate on the water basin. It's a living laboratory.

The library at Kulfo Campus is ridiculously small for a health sciences college. During exam season, it's completely full before 8 AM. It's a huge disadvantage when you live in a noisy, crowded dorm and have nowhere quiet to study.

The project-based learning at JIT is legit. You spend less time on boring theory and more time in the workshop actually building things. It's a practical, hands-on approach that really prepares you for an engineering career. The 'maker' culture is strong here.

I was skeptical about the mix of tech and agriculture at Tseda campus, but it's actually its greatest strength. We're working on innovative 'agri-tech' projects that feel incredibly relevant for the country's future. It's a very forward-thinking place.

It is ironic and disgusting that a health sciences campus like Atse Tewodros has such poor sanitation. The common bathrooms in the dorms are filthy and rarely maintained. It's a breeding ground for disease.

Despite all the recent hardships, there is a tangible sense of hope at Ayder campus. New collaborations with international partners are bringing in modern equipment and training opportunities for medical students. There's a strong collective will to rebuild and excel.

If you genuinely love agriculture and want to learn about it on a massive scale, Zenzelima is a paradise. The access to vast university farms and livestock is unmatched. This isn't for people looking for city life; it's for serious agriculturalists.

Yibab campus looks modern, but don't be fooled. The administration is just as slow, and many lecturers just read from outdated PowerPoint slides. The main selling point is its location, which is great for hanging out by the lake when you're skipping class.

The sheer number of students at Peda campus is overwhelming. Every space is crowded - classrooms, libraries, cafes. You feel like just a number, not an individual. It's easy to get lost in the crowd and hard to get personal attention from anyone.

The vet school at Debre Zeyit is excellent because it's so focused. Everyone around you—peers and professors—is dedicated to animal health. The large animal clinics are particularly good, offering experience you can't get anywhere else in the country.

EIABC is not a campus, it's a lifestyle. The 24/7 studio culture, the brutal critiques, the shared passion for design—it breaks you down and builds you back up. It is the most intense, exhausting, and rewarding experience of my life. Pure magic for aspiring architects.

The administration on the Debre Markos main campus seems to be allergic to technology. Registration is a week-long paper-chase, running between offices for signatures. It's an incredibly inefficient and frustrating system that wastes so much of the students' time.

We were sold a lie at Bichena. The university promised to upgrade this satellite campus and provide full-time staff. Nothing has materialized. We are being taught a limited curriculum by visiting lecturers. It's a fraudulent setup.

The worst thing about Chamo campus is the lecturer absenteeism. It is completely normal for instructors to simply not show up for class, with no warning or explanation. You can't get a consistent education when you don't even know if you'll have a class on any given day.

Kellamino is a very quiet campus. If your goal is to focus entirely on your veterinary studies with zero distractions, it might be the place for you. But there is absolutely no social life, no clubs, no events. It can be quite lonely.

Maraki is easily the best campus at UoG for student life. It's buzzing with energy, is close to all the best spots in Gondar, and the students here are very social. A great environment makes the stress of studying much more manageable. Absolutely love it here.

It is deeply ironic that the Institute of Water Technology has frequent and unpredictable water cuts on its own campus. It undermines the credibility of the institution and makes for a frustrating living situation.

Because Otona is a relatively small health campus, there's a strong sense of community. You know almost everyone in your year, and the lecturers are very approachable. It's a supportive environment, which is so important in a demanding field like medicine.

Calling Adi Haki a 'technology' campus is a bad joke. The internet is slower than a snail and cuts out constantly. How are we supposed to do research, code, or download essential software? It's a fundamental failure of the most basic requirement for a tech education.

Being at Kito Furdisa, away from the main city, is actually a blessing in disguise. The campus is new, clean, and quiet. It's a perfect environment to focus on your studies without the noise and distractions of the main campus.

One of the best things about the Gandaba main campus is the sports culture. The facilities are great, especially the football pitch and basketball courts. There are always tournaments happening, which creates a really fun and competitive atmosphere outside of class.

The best thing about studying at the Debre Markos main campus is the low cost of living. Compared to Addis Ababa, everything from food to private housing is incredibly affordable. It really reduces the financial stress on students.

The Gandaba campus is massive, and there's no shuttle service. I spend at least an hour every day just walking between my dorm, the cafeteria, and my lecture halls. It's exhausting and a huge waste of time.

Academic integrity is a joke at Burie campus. Cheating is widespread in exams, and the instructors turn a blind eye. It's deeply unfair to those of us who study honestly, and it makes me question the value of my degree.

The main library at Nekemte is a good, quiet place for studying, but that's about it. The book collection is terribly outdated. If you need any information published after the year 2000, you have to rely solely on your own internet data.

The power supply at Kito Furdisa is a disaster. The frequent, unannounced cuts and subsequent power surges have already fried my laptop's motherboard. How are we supposed to function as students in 2025 without reliable electricity for our devices?

As a graduate student in history, the resources at Peda Campus (AAU) are unmatched. The access to the Institute of Ethiopian Studies and various national archives located nearby is a priceless advantage for conducting serious research.

The lab equipment in the Biology and Chemistry departments at Arat Kilo is ancient. We're learning modern scientific principles but using equipment from the 1980s. It's impossible to conduct experiments properly, and it's a major handicap for our practical education.

The community at Yared School of Music is its greatest strength. It's a small school, so it feels more like a big family. We all know each other, support each other, and collaborate on performances. It's a wonderfully creative and non-competitive atmosphere.

Life at Bichena campus is incredibly monotonous. Your entire world is the triangle between your dorm, the classroom, and the cafeteria. There are no student clubs, no sports, no events—nothing. It's a very lonely and uninspiring place to spend your university years.

The Mechanical Engineering department at Bahir Dar's IoT is strong on theory, but weak on practice. There's a major disconnect from the actual industry. We have almost no factory visits, guest lectures from engineers, or internship support.

Look, if you get assigned to Shambu, you know what you're getting into. It's remote and there's nothing to do. If you can accept that and just want to put your head down, get your degree with minimal distractions, and leave, then it's manageable. Just don't expect a 'university experience'.

The resilience of the people in Mekelle is amazing. Despite everything they've been through, the local community is incredibly kind and supportive towards the students at Endayesus campus. It's a humbling and inspiring environment to be in.

Let's be honest about the Zenzelima campus: it's a giant farm. And with a huge dairy operation comes a very distinct smell. Most days you don't notice it, but when the wind blows the wrong way, it's overpowering.

The Public Health program at Atse Tewodros is outstanding because of the fieldwork. We spend a significant amount of time working in rural health posts around Gondar. This practical, community-based experience is far more valuable than any lecture.

Forget about online research or even calling your parents. The mobile network and internet connectivity at Gimbi campus is non-existent. You are completely cut off from the outside world. It's isolating and a massive academic disadvantage.

Academically, the medical program at the Harar campus is fine. It's a standard curriculum. The biggest challenge by far is the location. If you can mentally prepare for the isolation and logistical challenges, the education itself is adequate.

The atmosphere at the College of Health Sciences (Tikur Anbessa) is intensely competitive, and not always in a healthy way. It often feels like students are trying to tear each other down rather than collaborate. This high-stress, cutthroat environment can be very toxic.

There's a severe shortage of lecturers at the Otona health campus. We have the same instructor for three different major courses. They're clearly overworked, and we're not getting the specialized, in-depth teaching that we need and were promised.

The failed irrigation project on the Abaya campus farm is a running joke. They spent a fortune on a modern system that broke within a month. Now it just sits there, rusting. It's a perfect symbol of the incompetence in the campus administration.

The fresh milk, yogurt, and eggs produced by the university's own farms are a huge perk of being a student at Haramaya. It's high-quality, always available, and incredibly cheap. A small but significant boost to student life!

The Electrical and Computer Engineering department at Amist Kilo is exceptional. The curriculum is rigorous, up-to-date, and the professors are leaders in their fields. If you can survive the workload, you will graduate with a top-tier engineering education.

Trying to get to the School of Commerce for evening classes is a nightmare. The traffic around Mexico Square is horrendous, and there is absolutely no parking. You spend more time commuting and stressing than you do in the actual class.

Be warned: studying architecture at EIABC is extremely expensive. The cost of model-making supplies, plotter printing, and materials is astronomical, and you have to cover it all yourself. It adds a huge financial burden on top of the academic pressure.

The best thing about studying at Kulfo campus is our student-run community health projects. We regularly go to nearby rural areas to provide health education and basic screenings. It's incredibly fulfilling and provides invaluable practical experience.
If you are assigned to Dawro Tarcha campus, do everything in your power to get a transfer. My biggest regret is not fighting harder to leave. Please, save yourself.

Graduating from Arba Minch's Water Technology institute gives you a powerful advantage. The alumni network is spread throughout the country's water sector. It's a huge asset for finding jobs and building a career after graduation.

My macroeconomics class at Yibab campus has over 200 students. The lecturer stands at a podium with a microphone. There is no possibility for questions or discussion. You're not a student being taught; you're just an anonymous face in a lecture hall.

The vet campus itself is fine, but the town of Bishoftu (Debre Zeyit) is a real highlight. With its seven crater lakes and many resorts, it's a beautiful place to spend your weekends and de-stress from your studies.

Sidist Kilo feels safe during the day, but the campus is very dark at night due to poor lighting. Walking from the library back to the dorms late at night can feel quite unsafe, and there is little visible security presence.

While the academic facilities at Ayder are slowly recovering, the psychological impact of the war is still very present. Many students and staff are dealing with trauma, and the overall atmosphere is often heavy. It's a challenging environment that requires mental fortitude.

I was hesitant about coming to Nekemte, but joining the university's cultural club changed my entire experience. I found a vibrant community and made amazing friends. The people here are what make this campus a special place.

The dormitories on the Gimbi campus are infested with bedbugs. It's a chronic problem that the administration refuses to properly address. Getting a decent night's sleep is impossible, and it's taking a serious toll on my health and studies.

If you're coming to the main campus in Debre Markos, be prepared for the weather. It gets very cold and rains a lot, especially from June to September. The campus paths turn into mud, so good waterproof shoes are essential.

They've recently opened a few new dormitory blocks on the Burie campus, and they are a massive improvement over the old, dilapidated ones. It's a lottery whether you get placed in one, but it's a sign that some positive changes are happening.

As a female student, I do not feel safe on the Dawro Tarcha campus, especially after sunset. The campus is vast, poorly lit, and there is no visible security patrol. I avoid going to the library in the evening because the walk back to the dorm is terrifying.

The isolation of the Shambu campus is its best academic feature. With zero distractions, you can completely immerse yourself in your studies. If you are disciplined and self-motivated, this is a perfect environment to excel academically.

We are studying forestry in a literal forest at Wondo Genet, yet the lab equipment for soil and water analysis is decades old. It’s a beautiful location severely handicapped by outdated scientific tools. We can't perform the modern tests we read about in textbooks.

The best thing about the Harar health sciences campus is the focused community. Since we are all medical and health students, it creates a very supportive and collaborative environment. We form study groups easily and help each other through the tough curriculum.

The cafeteria food at Kulfo campus is appallingly monotonous. For the last month, the only options have been a watery shiro or macaroni with a thin tomato sauce. The lack of nutrition is a serious concern for students who rely on the cafe for all their meals.

JIT has a weird superiority complex. The students there act like they are separate from and better than the rest of Jimma University. There is very little interaction with the main campus, so you miss out on a lot of broader university events and culture.

The Tseda campus is a failed experiment. The 'technology' department is just a single room with a few outdated desktops, and the 'agriculture' section is a small, neglected plot of land. It's a ghost campus with no real resources. A complete waste of four years.

The anatomy lab at Atse Tewodros has a severe shortage of cadavers. There are far too many students per body, meaning most of us can only observe from a distance. This significantly compromises the quality of our practical medical training.

Just got to the Adi Haki campus for my freshman year. It feels really new and clean. The buildings are in great shape, and there's a good vibe among the students. I'm really excited to start my engineering classes here.

The veterinary training at Kellamino is almost exclusively focused on livestock like cows and goats. We get very little practical experience with companion animals. This is a huge gap in our education, especially for those who want to work in urban clinics.

The location of Maraki campus is a double-edged sword. It's great for having a social life in Gondar, but the noise from the city can be really distracting. If you're a light sleeper or need quiet to study, the dorms here are not ideal.

Just finished my first week at Peda campus. It's so big and crowded, I feel totally overwhelmed and anonymous. I'm just hoping I can figure out my way around and make some friends soon, because right now it feels very intimidating.

The exposure we get at EIABC is world-class. The school constantly brings in guest critics and lecturers from renowned international architecture firms. Hearing their perspectives and getting their feedback on our work is an invaluable part of the education here.

The registrar's office at Debre Markos main campus lost my official academic records. After making me run around for months, they finally admitted their fault but have no solution. Their incompetence is threatening my ability to graduate. I am beyond furious.

The student-led entrepreneurship club at Yibab campus is fantastic! We organize business plan competitions, invite successful local entrepreneurs for talks, and run workshops. It's a very practical and inspiring community for any aspiring business student.

One of the best aspects of the College of Development Studies is the diverse student body. My classmates are from all over the continent, working for different NGOs and governments. The discussions in class are incredibly rich and insightful.

I was terrified when I was assigned to Bichena campus, but it's been surprisingly okay. It's a very small community, so you get to know all your classmates and teachers personally. If you can handle a very, very quiet life, it's manageable.

The pace of life at Chamo campus is very relaxed, much like Arba Minch town itself. It's a beautiful, low-stress environment to pursue your degree. Having Nech Sar National Park and the lakes right on our doorstep for weekend trips is a massive plus.

For an institute of 'water technology,' our curriculum is far too theoretical. We spend hours on calculations but get very little hands-on time in the lab with modern hydraulic pumps, pipes, or water quality testing equipment. We need more practical skills.

I am about to graduate, and I owe everything to my time at Otona. The instructors were more than teachers; they were mentors who supported and challenged me. I am leaving here as a competent and confident health professional, ready to serve my community. Thank you, Otona.

The academic programs on the main agriculture campus are strong, but the dormitories are in a state of decay. Leaky roofs, broken windows, and a constant battle with pests are the norm. The living conditions desperately need to be addressed.

The psychology curriculum at the College of Education feels very disconnected from our reality. Most of the theories and case studies are from Western contexts and aren't critically adapted to fit Ethiopian social and cultural realities. It feels like we're learning about someone else's problems.

Being a female engineering student at Amist Kilo can be challenging. It's a very male-dominated environment, and you sometimes have to fight to be heard or taken seriously in group projects. It's not overt, but there's a definite 'boys' club' culture.

A huge plus for Hawassa's IoT campus is how well-designed and maintained it is. The grounds are clean, the buildings are modern, and there are pleasant outdoor spaces to study or relax. It creates a positive atmosphere that makes you feel proud to be a student there.

The library at Ayder is still struggling to recover. So many books and journals were lost or destroyed during the conflict. The digital resources are also very limited, making it incredibly difficult to do proper research or study for exams.

I just moved into my dorm at Gandaba as a freshman. It's super crowded and a bit chaotic, but the senior students in my block have been incredibly welcoming and helpful. Despite the madness, it already feels like we're one big, crazy family.

Living in the historic dorms at Sidist Kilo is not as romantic as it sounds. It's like living in a crumbling museum with terrible plumbing and leaky ceilings. The sense of history is cool for a day, but trying to live and study in these conditions for years is awful.

Just graduated from Amist Kilo and landed a great job at a major tech company. The interviewer told me they prefer graduates from here because they know we can handle immense pressure and complex problems. The brutal workload was 100% worth it.

The evening program at the School of Commerce is perfectly designed for people like me who work during the day. The central location is easy to get to after work, and the professors are understanding of the challenges of balancing a full-time job with studies.

My first week at Wondo Genet has been magical. I woke up this morning to the sound of colobus monkeys in the trees outside my dorm. This campus is a literal paradise. I cannot believe I get to study in the middle of a forest for the next four years!

The instructors at Yared are true masters, some are living legends of Ethiopian music. You come here for their knowledge. However, you have to constantly battle a disorganized administration and underfunded facilities. It's a frustrating mix of brilliance and bureaucracy.

The water situation on the main Nekemte campus is beyond a joke. We have not had a single drop of running water in our dormitory block for four consecutive days. Not low pressure, not intermittent—completely dry taps. It's a sanitary crisis.

The town of Gimbi itself is very small and quiet, with not much to offer students in terms of entertainment. You really have to make your own fun on campus with your friends. The local people are friendly, though.

Why does the library on the Shambu campus close at 8 PM? It's the only quiet place to study on the entire campus. For a university, the limited library access is a major obstacle to our education, especially during exam season.

The food served in the Harar campus cafeteria is not just poor quality, it's dangerous. Myself and several of my friends have gotten sick with food poisoning after eating there. It's a health sciences campus with a kitchen that is a public health hazard.

The clinical skills lab at Kulfo is excellent. It's new, modern, and has high-quality mannequins for us to practice on. Being able to rehearse procedures like injections and suturing in the lab first makes you much more confident when you work with real patients.

Studying at Atse Tewodros campus feels special. You are learning medicine in a place with such a deep and long history of healing in Ethiopia. The old hospital building is a constant source of inspiration.

My father was a patient at Ayder Hospital recently. The dedication, kindness, and professionalism of the medical students who were part of his care team were incredible. They are a beacon of hope for the future and a true credit to their university.

The best part of Zenzelima is that we're not just reading from books. As a veterinary student, I'm out in the barns with the university's dairy herd almost every day. That kind of consistent, hands-on experience is something you can't put a price on.

There is a professor in the Yibab campus accounting department who forces students to buy his ridiculously priced, self-published handouts. If you don't buy them, you are almost guaranteed to fail his course. It's blatant corruption and everyone knows about it.

The Maritime Engineering program at Bahir Dar's IoT is amazing. Where else in the world can you say your classroom is one of Africa's largest lakes? The practical sessions on Lake Tana are the highlight of my week, every week.

I was feeling a bit lost at Peda until I joined the university debate club. Now I have a community. There are so many student clubs and associations here, you just have to make a little effort to find your people.

The curriculum at the Debre Zeyit vet school feels stagnant. We're learning techniques and using textbooks from 20 years ago, with very little mention of modern diagnostic tools or treatments. The program needs a serious update to stay relevant.

While the EIABC campus is amazing, finding affordable housing in the Lideta area is a huge challenge. The rent is extremely high, forcing many of us to commute for over an hour each way. This is especially draining given the long hours we spend in the studio.

My four years at Debre Markos University were... fine. Just fine. The education was adequate. The campus was okay. The town was okay. Nothing was terrible, but nothing was exciting either. It was a completely forgettable experience.

I was worried about being assigned to Burie, but I actually love it. Because the campus and town are so small, you create a very tight-knit community. Everyone knows everyone, and there's a real sense of looking out for each other. It feels like home.
This place is an academic black hole from which no light or knowledge can escape.

They call Maraki the 'social campus', but that just means it's impossible to get any peace and quiet. There's loud music blasting from dorms at all hours of the day and night. The administration does nothing to enforce quiet hours for studying.

The academic program at Chamo is just average, but the location is five-star. I've spent my weekends exploring the forty springs, watching the crocs and hippos, and hiking in the mountains. My degree feels like an excuse to live in a tourist destination.

Because Kellamino is a small and remote campus, the professors are incredibly accessible. They live on campus and their doors are always open if you need help. The student-to-faculty ratio is excellent, and you get a lot of personal attention.

I'm cautiously optimistic about Tseda campus. A new dean just started who seems very motivated. They've already secured funding to build a new computer lab and hire more staff. It feels like things might finally start to improve.

I'm writing this as a parent. My son was placed at the Bichena campus. He has no qualified teachers for his major courses and no library with relevant books. This campus is a betrayal of our children's futures. We are doing everything we can to get him transferred.

I came from Kenya specifically for the MSc in Water Resource Management at AMU, and it has been a fantastic decision. The level of expertise among the faculty is truly world-class. It is a leading institution in the field, without a doubt.

Commuting to Kito Furdisa campus from Jimma town is a daily struggle. The public transport is infrequent and unreliable, especially in the evening. If you have a class that ends late, getting back home can be a real problem.

Just got back to Otona for my third year. The campus hasn't changed much, but Sodo town has really grown. There are more cafes, restaurants, and shops now, which is a nice improvement and gives us more options off-campus.

It's the first week of the new semester at Gandaba, and the one machine that prints student ID cards is broken. We can't enter the library, computer labs, or even some classroom buildings without a valid ID. This exact same thing happens every single year. Incompetence.

Just got back to Peda for my final year. The campus is still soaked and muddy from the kiremt rains, but the air is fresh. The chaos of registration is already starting near the registrar's office. Here we go again.

I just arrived at Gandaba campus for the freshman remedial program. It's HUGE and a bit confusing to navigate! But some senior students were kind enough to show me to my dorm. Feeling nervous but optimistic!

Back at Ayder for my clinical rotations. The hospital seems busier than ever, and you can see the strain on the staff and resources. The resilience here is incredible, but it's going to be a challenging year for all of us.

Returned to my dorm at Nekemte to find it full of mold. They clearly didn't secure the windows properly during the rainy season. The administration is useless. What a disgusting and depressing way to start the semester.
So happy to be back at Wondo Genet after the break. The entire campus is incredibly lush and vibrant after the long rains. It's the most beautiful time of year here. It feels good to be home.
First night back on the main campus in Debre Markos, and the power has already been out for three hours. Some things never change. At least I missed the coffee from the local cafes.

Kicking off my final year project at JIT. The workshops are already buzzing with activity as students are getting started. The pressure is definitely on, but we have access to the best facilities. Let's get this done.

I just dropped my daughter off at the Burie campus. As a parent, I'm quite concerned. The facilities look very basic, and the town is so small. It's hard leaving her in a place with so few resources, so far from home.
The dirt road leading to the Harar health sciences campus is a muddy disaster after the rainy season. It makes the campus feel even more isolated than it already is. Not a great welcome back.

The pressure at Amist Kilo is immediate. I haven't even fully unpacked my bags and my classmates are already forming study groups for courses that don't start for another week. There's no time to relax here.

It’s good to be back at Yibab campus. The view of Lake Tana is spectacular with the water level so high after the rains. Ready for a new semester of studying economics and relaxing by the water on weekends.

My transfer request out of Shambu was denied, so I'm back here for another year. The feeling of dread returning to this remote campus with nothing to do is indescribable. Counting down the days until I can leave for good.
My parents just dropped me off at the Hawassa IoT campus. I'm a mix of nervous and incredibly excited. The campus is so modern and well-kept! Looking forward to orientation week.
Back in the studio at EIABC for my final thesis year. I know it's going to be a year of sleepless nights and constant work, but the creative energy is already amazing. This place is my second home.

Just starting the pre-med program at the College of Health Sciences. The orientation was packed. The sheer number of students is intimidating. I feel like a tiny fish in a massive, hyper-competitive ocean.

Walking through Sidist Kilo for my last 'first day' as a final year student. Feeling very nostalgic. This campus has many flaws, but its historic atmosphere is something special. I'm actually going to miss this place.

Returned to Maraki campus, and it's already loud and buzzing with activity. This is great for my social life but terrible for my bank account, as all the cafes and clubs in Gondar are calling my name.

Back on the Gimbi campus. There's a noticeable tension in the air again. Students are whispering about potential security problems in the region. It's hard to feel optimistic about an uninterrupted semester.

I was placed at Dawro Tarcha last year. It was a complete nightmare. I fought the administration for months and finally got a transfer. To any new students assigned there: do not accept it. It is not a real university experience.

The unpaved paths at Zenzelima are a sea of mud after the kiremt season. You need a solid pair of boots just to get from the dorms to the lecture halls without slipping. They really need to invest in some basic paving.
So happy to be back at Otona. The best part of a smaller campus is seeing all your friends on the very first day you get back. It's a genuinely close-knit community to return to after the break.

First week back at Arba Minch's main campus. The view of the 'Bridge of God' between the two lakes is stunning with the water so full from the rain. Unfortunately, the campus Wi-Fi is as slow as the crocodiles sunbathing on the shore.

The dorm situation at Kulfo is worse this year. They've squeezed an extra bunk bed into our already small room. Five of us are now living in a space designed for three. It's going to be a long, cramped year.

Starting my final year at the vet school in Debre Zeyit. The practical work with the local farmers and their animals has been the most valuable part of my education. I'm ready to get back into the clinics and make the most of this last year.

It's the end of August, and the registration line at the School of Commerce already snakes around the building. You waste the entire first week of the semester just standing in lines. The administration is unbelievably inefficient.

Just moved into my dorm near the Arat Kilo campus. The area is so energetic and full of students. The campus buildings look old, but you can feel the history of science and learning. I'm so excited to start my physics degree here.

A word of warning for new students at Abaya campus: the mosquitoes after the rainy season are no joke. Make sure you have a good, intact bed net from day one, or you will be eaten alive at night. The university should really do more about pest control.

YES! So happy to be back at Chamo! The weather is perfect, the view is incredible, and I'm ready for another year of 'intense studying' by the lake. This is without a doubt the best campus location in Ethiopia.

I'm a freshman who just arrived at the Kito Furdisa campus. It's much newer and cleaner than I expected, but it also feels very far from the main town of Jimma. I'm a bit worried about feeling isolated during my first year away from home.

Just returned to Endayesus campus for my third year. There are definitely more students around compared to this time last year. The campus is starting to feel more alive and vibrant. It's really good to see it slowly coming back to its former self.
First Friday night of the semester at Maraki and the campus is absolutely buzzing! It's so good to be back and see everyone. This campus has the best energy in Gondar. The city is alive tonight!

It’s my first Friday night away from my family, and I'm in my dorm room at Shambu campus. The silence is overwhelming. There’s no internet, no TV, nothing to do. I’m already feeling incredibly lonely.
Trying to get a head start on my reading tonight at Peda, but it's impossible. The noise from the dorm common areas is insane. I guess everyone is celebrating being back. Wish I could focus.

It is 9 PM on a Friday, and I'm still trying to resolve my dormitory assignment issue. The admin office closed hours ago, leaving me and about ten other students with nowhere to sleep tonight. This is a horrible welcome.

A quiet Friday night in the lab at Amist Kilo. It's the perfect time to calibrate my equipment for my final year project before the campus is swarming with undergrads next week. The grind here never really stops, even before day one.
Just chilling with friends at a cafe near Yibab campus. The air is cool and fresh after the rainy season. It's so good to be back in Bahir Dar. This is the best city to be a student in.

It's my first Friday night at Gandaba. My new dorm mates are pretty cool, and we've just been sitting around talking about our homes and what we expect from uni. It's a bit strange, but it's much better than being alone.
The highlight of my Friday night in Burie? The electricity came back on after a three-hour blackout. That’s the peak of excitement on this campus.

Walking back to my dorm on the Nekemte campus a few minutes ago was unsettling. Half of the main pathways are in complete darkness because the lights are broken. It feels very unsafe, especially with so many new people around.

It's Friday night, and I'm already in the studio at EIABC setting up my workspace for the semester. The place is already half-full of other students doing the same. The social life of an architecture student is just... different.
My first Friday night on-call for the new semester at Ayder Hospital. It’s hectic, but this is the real-world experience I came here for. No time for parties when you're saving lives.
The main entertainment on the Harar campus on a Friday night is watching the wild hyenas from a safe distance as they gather outside the main gate. The isolation here is no joke.

It's beautifully peaceful at Wondo Genet tonight. Just the sounds of the forest and the river. It's perfect for relaxing, but a small part of me wishes there was a bit more excitement on a Friday night.

My friends on the main campus are all going out in Jimma town tonight. I'm stuck here at Kito Furdisa because getting transport back this late is impossible. Really wishing I was on the main campus right now.
Just left the JFK library at Sidist Kilo. It's 9 PM on a Friday and it was still packed with students. The academic pressure at AAU is real, and the semester hasn't even officially begun.

The senior students at Hawassa IoT organized a welcome bonfire for us freshmen tonight! There's music playing and everyone is just hanging out and getting to know each other. This place already feels like a great community. So happy I was placed here!
There's a sort of unofficial curfew on the Gimbi campus due to the security situation. Everyone makes sure to be back in their dorms by nightfall. So much for having a social life on a Friday night.
My Friday night entertainment at Dawro Tarcha consists of listening to the campus generator sputter and die, plunging us into darkness. Again. I despise this place.

It's a quiet Friday night here at Zenzelima. A few of us are playing cards in the common room. It's not the wild university life you see in movies, but it's peaceful. You have to make your own community here.

Just had a fantastic 'welcome back' buna with my professor and lab mates at a small cafe near Arat Kilo. The intellectual community here is what makes it special. I'm energized and ready to tackle some complex physics this year.
Just finished a late-night study session with my nursing group at Otona. We have a placement test first thing on Monday. The grind starts early here, but at least we all support each other.
Friday night at Bichena. I have read the only two novels I brought from home. Now I am staring at the wall. The boredom on this campus is a physical entity.
Sitting by the shore of Lake Abaya near the campus. It's a beautiful, starry night. The view is amazing, but the mosquitoes are eating me alive. The perfect metaphor for this campus.
First Friday back at Chamo, and there's a bonfire on the beach! We're all just chilling, playing music. This is exactly why this campus is the best. The lifestyle is unbeatable.
Just finished my late-night checks on the animals in the Kellamino clinic. This is my Friday night. The work is meaningful, but a part of me wishes I was in a more lively place.
The air at Haramaya is so cool and fresh tonight. Just taking a long walk around the beautiful, quiet campus with some friends. A perfect, peaceful start to the semester.

It's Friday night and I'm supposed to be relaxing, but instead I'm trying to register for my courses online and the Tseda campus portal keeps crashing. The 'technology' part of this campus is an absolute joke.
Just got back to my dorm near the College of Education. The area is pretty quiet on a Friday night, which I appreciate. If you're here to actually study and not party, it's a good location.

My wallet was stolen from my dorm room at Kulfo campus tonight while I was taking a shower. The doors don't lock properly and there is zero security presence. I don't feel safe here. A terrible start to the year.

The welcome-back reception for graduate students at the College of Development Studies tonight was fantastic. I've already met fascinating people working on impactful projects all over the continent. The networking opportunities here are incredible.

It's Friday night at Yared, and the air is filled with the sound of kirar, masinko, and pianos drifting from the practice rooms. This is our kind of party. The creative energy on this campus is everything.
